REPORT 
 
BRIEF BACKGROUND 
Indian culture and heritage is one of the oldest and richest in the world, dating back to 
several millennia. It is a diverse blend of various customs, beliefs, traditions, and values that 
have evolved over time and have been shaped by different religions, languages, and historical 
events. India's cultural and spiritual heritage is reflected in its architecture, literature, music, 
dance, cuisine, and festivals, which continue to fascinate and inspire people from all over the 
world. From the ancient Indus Valley civilization to the present day, Indian culture has 
witnessed numerous influences and transformations. This makes it a unique and dynamic 
tapestry of humanity's collective experience. 
2. Broadly, this Ministry is working on the protection, development and promotion of all 
types of Heritage and Culture namely, Tangible Heritage, Intangible Heritage and 
Knowledge Heritage. In addition, the Ministry also harbour s the responsibility of Gandhian 
Heritage and Commemoration of important historical events and centenaries of great 
personalities. 
3. Major programmes/activities of the Ministry of Culture relating to promotion, 
dissemination, preservation and conservation of the cultural heritage of the country are being 
implemented through a network of two attached offices, six subordinate offices, one statutory 
body, thirty-three Autonomous organisations and one charitable trust under its control. The 
Ministry also implements schemes for promotion and dissemination of Art and Culture under 
umbrella(s) namely; Centenaries & Anniver saries Scheme, Kala Sanskriti Vi kas Yojna, 
Development of Museum, Development of Libraries & Archives, Global Engagement & 
International Coopera tion and National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Roadmap. 
Activities of National Gandhi Heritage Site Mission are undertaken through Kala Sanskriti 
Vikas Yojna. The Ministry has no Centrally Sponsored Schemes.

THE MINISTRY  
B.E. 2023-24: Salient features and Projected Demand vs Allocation

crore, consisting of Rs. 3114.25 crore under Revenue and Rs. 285.40 crore under Capital 
heads for undertaking various prioritized programmes/activities/projects. This budgetary 
allocation is about 12.98% more than the budgetary provisions at BE 2022-23. The projected 
demand of the Ministry for 2023-24 was 3989.18 crore.

allocation for 2023 -24 along with allocation made by the Ministry of Culture under each

2023-24, and  upon analysing the expenditure trend of FY 2022 -23, it has ensured an optimal 
distribution of funds across various sectors in FY 2023 -24. It furnished the follow ing 
information with regard to the shortfall in allocation:

8. The Ministry stated that it would have to reorient its activities in such a way that 
important activities would not suffer for want of funds in the Year 2023 -24. However, it is 
expected that deficiency in funds ,if any, would be adequately addressed by the Ministry of 
Finance through an advance from the contingency fund of India/at  the supplementary stage/ 
at the Revised Estimate stage of FY 2023-24. 
 
9. The Committee noted that the allocation  for the Ministry of Culture is just 0.075% of 
the total budget this year. This is in sharp contrast to countries such as China, the UK, the 
USA, Singapore and Australia, which spend roughly 2 – 5% of their budget on the promotion 
of arts and culture.  
 
10. In response, the Ministry stated that it may not be tenable for a developing nation like 
India to allocate a considerable proportion of its public fund in the area of promotion of art 
and culture given the high disparity it experiences in elementary ru ral infrastructures like 
health, education and transportation etc. as against the countries in comparison. However, 
this Ministry has been consistently able to increase its budgetary outlays over the years 
except in the Covid pandemic period where priority  was given to other social sector 
ministries.  Though the approved budget outlay for the Ministry is a relative increase with 
respect to the previous financial year, the Ministry had projected around Rs. 3989 crore as a 
result of an overwhelming increase i n the number of activities by all organisations/offices 
under the ambit of Ministry of Culture. This is an achievable budget at RE 2023 -24 stage 
provided a good pace of expenditure is maintained in the next FY as well.  It may also be 
noted that apart from the union government spending on the promotion of arts and culture, a 
considerable part of the public spending is also made by the state governments in the field of 
art and culture which is not captured in the overall spent. 
11. The Ministry further menti oned that while a majority of the amount spent on art and 
culture is from the non -government sources for the counties in comparison, this may not be 
true for our county. Hence, the Ministry is trying and evolving innovative methods to 
maximise the particip ation of non -government organisations in the field of promotion and 
conservation of art and culture. Monument Mitra, NCF etc. are examples of such initiatives. 
This Ministry believes that Culture should be an area where a large part of expenditure needs 
to be sourced from non -government sources. Moreover, the Ministry of culture is taking a 
phenomenal role in supporting non -governmental organisations/voluntary organisations 
through its schemes/ organisations for participating in overall propagation, preserv ation and 
promotion of all forms of art and culture. This can be considered to have a ripple effect on 
the budget utilised by the Ministry. 
12. An year-on-year increase of BE is depicted in the table below:

13. The Committee notes that the Ministry has been awarded 85 percent of its 
projected demand for BE 2023 -24. The shortfall in demand versus allocation has 
increased from 11 percent at BE stage in 2022 -23 to 15 percent in 2023 -24. Moreover, 
the allocation made  to various Central Sector Schemes is much lower vis -à-vis the 
demand of the Ministry. This includes allocations under Support to Akademies (63.9% 
of demand), Support to Museums (76.1%), Support to Libraries (70%) and Buddhist 
Tibetan Institutions and Memo rials (62.8%). These heads support the expenditure of 
various autonomous bodies such as Sangeet Natak Akademi, Indian Museum (Kolkata), 
Delhi Public Library, Central Institute of Buddhist Studies. The Committee desires to 
be apprised of the broad impact of  the shortfall on the activities of the various 
autonomous bodies under these heads.  
14. The Ministry of Culture shoulders the crucial responsibility of the preservation, 
development and promotion of the country's tangible as well as intangible heritage. 
Keeping this in mind, the Committee is convinced that the BE allocation of 3399.65 
crores for 2022-23 does not suffice the fund requirements of the Ministry. This is likely 
to adversely affect the vital projects, activities and schemes planned by the Minis try for 
2023-24.  
15. The allocation of Rs. 3399 crores for BE 2023 -24 is ~13 percent higher than BE 
2022-23 and ~1 percent higher than RE 2022 -23. However, the Committee notes that 
the increase of 1 percent as compared to RE 2022 -23 is not sufficient to c over the 
impact of inflation. The spending power of the Ministry will actually decrease in 2023 -
24.  
16. The Committee also takes note of the year -on-year change in the budgetary 
allocation of the Ministry. The budget of the Ministry has increased from ₹2169 crores 
in 2015-16 to ~ ₹3400 crores in 2023 -24, an increase of 57 percent. In comparison, the 

Page 6 of 142 
 
total budget of the Government in this period has risen from ₹17.77 lakh crores to 
₹45.03 lakh crore, an increase of 153 percent. 
17. In view of these observations, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
underscore the importance of its mandated duties to the Ministry of Finance for higher 
allocation at R.E. stage. Ministry of Finance may be requested to minimise the shortfall 
in allocation vis-à-vis the projected demand. The Ministry may also ensure that the 
funds allocated to it are fully utilised to permit higher allocations at future stages. 
18. The Committee agrees with the submission that a majority of the amount spent 
on art and culture in many countries is from non -government sources. The Committee 
suggests that the Ministry should increase its focus on encouraging private 
participation in the art and culture sector.  
19. The Ministry should try to attract investment from private organisati ons under 
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds, besides seeking investments through 
Public Private Partnership (PPP) route. Private sector's active participation will help 
the Ministry reach the desired level of investment in India's Culture and Her itage 
sector. This would enable much better preservation and development of monuments 
and museums in the country. It would also help India become a more attractive tourist 
destination. 
20. As regards new projects/ schemes planned by the Ministry for the ye ar 2023-24, the 
Ministry stated that its  six Central Sector Schemes would be continued in FY 2023 -24 and 
sufficient funds have been allocated in this sector. An additional Rs. 11 crore for G20 related 
expenses are allocated for the Ministry. Sufficient fun ds are also allocated to the project “Art 
work in the new Parliament Building” which commenced in the FY 2022 -23 and is planned 
to be completed by FY 2023 -24. New projects like “Gokhale hall”, “Kedarnath 
redevelopment” etc . are planned for FY 2023 -24. It i s reiterated that all efforts would be 
made so that deficiency in funds would be adequately addressed through an advance from 
CFI/ at supplementary stage/ at Revised Estimate stage of FY 2023-24. 
21. The Committee appreciates the assurance given by the Min istry that no activity 
will be compromised for want of funds. 
22. From the year 2023 -24 onwards, the Ministry of Finance has further classified the 
budget heads under Revenue and Capital section. This classification has further rationalised 
the expenditure under both sections of expenditure. For e.g. the ‘Head -01 Salary, Sumptuary 
allowances’ has been segregated and the components like LTC, Dearness allowances etc. 
which were part of the salary have been put under new budget heads.  Similarly, ‘Office 
expenses -13’ under revenue has been further rationalised and new heads have been created 
for a number of items of expenditure which are components of this head at present. With the

expansion and use of IT/digitization in the day to day life and official activ ities, the head 
which is being used to gather information on IT is presently under Revenue section only. In 
the new classification the same has been bifurcated in both the section of expenditure 
depending on the cost and longevity of the equipment purchase d under machinery & 
equipment head and under ICT. Under the Capital section ‘Major works -53’, the expenditure 
presently captures the expenditure as codified in CPWD code. In the revised classification, 
this head has been done away w.e.f. 2023 -24 and seven separate heads have been created 
under the Capital section of Expenditure. Several other new budgetary heads have been 
created in the revenue section from 2023 -24. Classification of the new Budget heads would 
capture a crystallised picture of expenditure in both sections from 2023-24. 
 
23. In its meeting held on 15 th February, 2023, the Committee noted that in BE 2023 -24, 
₹3114 crores  has been allocated towards revenue while only ₹285 crores is towards capital 
expenditure. As regards the adequacy of the ca pital allocation, the Secretary, MoC informed 
that allocation made to autonomous bodies is given under revenue head even though part of 
the funds is spent for capital works. The total amount spent on capital purposes was Rs. 750 
crores out of Rs. 3,400 crores in 2022-23. The Ministry expects capital expenditure for 2023-
24 to be around Rs. 1,000 crores in 2023 -24.He highlighted that this is an accounting 
anomaly and assured that the Ministry will try to have it corrected. 
 
24. The Committee notes that Capital investments generate future cash flows for the 
national economy. Capital figures are factored into macroeconomic indicators such as 
Capex-to-GDP. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the expenditure made for 
capital purposes should be correctly ref lected in the budget figures. The Ministry may 
ensure that this accounting anomaly is corrected as soon as possible.  
 
Expenditure under various heads in the ongoing Financial Year 2022-23 
25. The approved outlay of the Ministry for 2022 -23 was Rs.3009.05 crore. At RE 2022 -
23 stage the outlay has been increased to Rs.3363.07 crore. Against the approved outlay, the 
Ministry has incurred an expenditure of Rs. 2302.74 crore by 31 January 2023. Sect or-wise

26. The Ministry highlighted the peculiar nature of the expenditure pattern made by the 
offices/ organisations working under MoC through the following points: 
  
27. The budget of the Ministry of Culture is essentially an institution-based one. From the 
table above, it is clear that a major portion of the budgetary allocation of the Ministry is 
distributed to its 2 Attached Offices,  6 Subordinate offices and 34 Autonomous

one-third of the total Revenue allocation of the Ministry. Archaeological Survey of India 
spends a substantial portion of its f unds regularly on Conservation and Preservation of 
Monuments, as also on new excavation projects. Archaeological Survey of India is in a 
position to incur large sums of expenditure only after the monsoon season is over every year. 
As the Centrally Protected Monuments are spread all over the country, the work relating to 
their upkeep, conservation, preservation and peripheral development get affected in an 
adverse manner during the monsoon season, resulting in slow progress of budgetary 
expenditure during this period (first two quarters). 
28. The Ministry of Culture extends financial assistance under various schemes in the 
form of Grant -in-aid to institutions / voluntary cultural organizations and individuals 
including fellowships to Artists Pension regularly . These beneficiaries are extended financial 
assistance on the basis of recommendations / approval of the Expert Committees / Finance 
Committees constituted for the purpose under each scheme. The time gap of procedural 
formalities such as constitution of t hese Expert Committees, meetings of the Committees, 
finalization of eligible beneficiary institutions/individuals on the recommendations of these 
Committees and release of grants to the eligible institutions / individuals could be very well 
appreciated. Th e procedural formalities which take time, lead to slow pace of expenditure 
normally during the initial quarters of FY. 
29. Exhibitions / Festivals are organized by the Ministry of Culture during the last two 
quarters of the financial year leading to higher  expenditure during this period under the 
budget sub-heads as compared to the previous two quarters. 
30. Moreover, this year four out of the six CS schemes of the Ministry had to be migrated 
to the CNA model for release of funds. The Ministry faced a lot o f technical constraints 
which affected the smooth flow of funds under these schemes and thereby expenditure was 
not booked as anticipated. 
31. The Ministry stated that it had nonetheless made its best effort to allocate and incur 
expenditure in such a mann er that it adhered to the cash management guidelines issued by 
Ministry of Finance for better fiscal discipline. Till 3 rd quarter of FY 2022 -23, the Ministry 
had incurred an expenditure of Rs. 2006.9 crs as against the allocation of Rs.3009.05 crore. 
Moreover, an amount of Rs. 107.37 crore was utilised by this time from Contingency Fund of 
India, which had resulted in a total expenditure of Rs. 2114.28 crore  (70.26% of BE 2022 -
23). 
  
32. However, at the RE stage of FY 2022 -23, the budget of the Ministry was  revised and 
an additional Rs. 354.02 crore was approved. Hence, there would be a higher expenditure in 
the last quarter mostly due to the upward revision of funds in RE 2022-23.

43. The Committee appreciates the good progress made by the Ministry in meeting a 
majority of the targets set under the Output Outcome Framework. The Committee 
notes that in many cases such as the number of gurus and artists financially supported,

that the Ministry may duly factor in the achievements of the previous year and set 
higher targets for the next year, as may be permitted by the available allocations. 
44. The Committee notes that the pace of progress under some important output

Scheme, number of Museum and Library professionals trained, number of 
programmes conducted for promotion of culture of science, and so on . The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may look into the reasons  for under -achievement of 
targets in each such case. The bottlenecks being faced in achieving the targets may be 
effectively addressed to ensure higher pace of progress in the FY 2023-24.

related activities are allowed only with prior permission from Competent Authority/ National

and many times such type matters also go into litigations thereby further delaying the

● Reprography and Computer Centre of the National Library:  Reprography

newspapers, documents, manuscripts in the form of digitization and microfilm.

National Library performs the works of chemical treatment of books that are more brittle and 
not in a condition of use. These books will be applied to a chemical treatment known as de -
acidification (Aqueous and Non- aqueous process). Thereafter, these books will be laminated 
(solvent and tissue process). 
● Preservation (Binding)  Division of the National Library: The Preservation 
(Binding) division of the National Library performs the works of binding, mending and other 
related works for the preservation of the books and newspapers. The process is a continuous 
process. The binding , mending and other related works for the old, brittle and rare books, 
journals and periodicals is being taken as a continuous process both in -house as well as 
outsourcing of services. 
● Rare Book Division of the National Library: The general rare books are 
placed in compactor alcoves with rubber linings that are placed on tracks for better utilisation 
of the space and giving books a sealed and compact environment when closed. The over -
sized books are kept in almirahs with larger space to better adjust the bo oks in the shelves 
maintaining relative humidity. Temperature of the Rare Books stack area is maintained 
below 21 degrees Celsius. The relative humidity of the Rare Books stack area is maintained 
around 40%.

REPORT 
 
Shipping is the life  blood of the global economy. Shipping‟s ability to transport goods 
cheaply, in large volumes and with the minimum environmental footprint is unmatched by any 
other mode of transportation. Around 80% of the international trade in goods is carried by sea. 
The importance of maritime trade has been underscored in recent times by the Covid Pandemic 
which disrupted suppl y chains and shipping networks.  The trade loss due to delay s in cargo 
shipments, higher shipping costs and lower m aritime connectivity lead to higher inflation and 
shortage of food and adversely impact the  world economy. Maritime Transport is a critical 
infrastructure for the economic development of a country. It influences the pace, structure and 
pattern of development.  
2. The Maritime sector in India comprises Ports, Shipping, Ship Building, Ship Repair and 
Inland Water Systems. India has a long coastline of about 7,500 kilometers spread on the western 
and eastern shelves of the mainland and also along  the islands with 12 government-owned major 
ports and approximately 200 minor and intermediate ports dotting the coastline.  Around 95% of 
the country‟s trade by volume and 68% by value is moved through Maritime Transport.  India is 
also endowed with 14500 kilometers of in land waterways in the form of rivers, canals, 
backwaters and creeks. The geographical location of India is at the centre of the Indian Ocean 
which is the epicenter of economic activity due to key international trade routes  which give 
strategic advantage to  India. Shipping is therefore a vital part of the Indian economy. As Prime 
Minister Narendra Modi summed it up succinctly, the blue chakra or wheel in India's national 
flag represents the potential of Blue Revolution or the Ocean Economy and that is how ce ntral 
the Ocean Economy is to India.

11. The budget provision is for development of coastal community, assistance for creation of 
infrastructure to promote  the movement of cargo/passengers by S ea/National Waterways,

domestic waterways (inland and coastal) in  the modal mix, generate logistic cost saving s, boost 
merchandize export s and create new jobs.  This also includes projects for the development of 
minor ports.

tune of Rs. 190 Crore under the Sagarmala Schemes and Projects.  The Committee observes that 
Sagarmala Schemes and Projects are very vital for the development of the Indian Maritime 
Sector.  The Committee was not provided with any reason for the Ministry of Finance‟s dissent 
to the proposal of the MoPS&W.

ABSORPTIVE CAPACITY OF B.E. 2023-24 ALLOCATIONS 
17. Upon query regarding the absorptive capacity of B.E. 2023 -24 allocations, the Ministry 
has submitted that this may pertain to two Budgetary Heads – Assistance to Ship Building and 
Inland Waterways.  In the case of Budgetary Head – Assistance to Ship Building, the projections 
are based on the demand of Indian shipyards in light of delivery of their vessels.  The entire fund 
can be utilized if shipyards deliver their vessels on schedu led time.   The Ministry has added that 
increased allocation under the Revenue and Capital Heads is of Rs. 10.07 crores and Rs. 5 crores 
respectively, hence the increase is marginal. 
18. Regarding Inland Waterways, the Ministry has stated that the enhanced exp enditure 
would be used for the completion of newly sanctioned and ongoing projects at NW -1 and NW -
2 and Phase-I development of NW-3,4, 5 and 13 new NWs sanctioned last year.  
19. The Ministry has also stated that the enhanced BE 2023 -24 of Rs. 250.10 crore a llocated 
towards dredging subsidy given to Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port as compared to RE 2022 -23 of 
Rs. 195.10 crore has been made in terms of DIB approval of DoE vide 25(15)/PF -II/2009 dt. 
23.2.2021 
20. The Committee notes that B.E. 2023-24 has an increase of 23.7%  over R.E. 2022-23, 
an increase of Rs. 425.37 crores.  The Ministry has not proposed to introduce any new 
scheme in the F.Y. 2023 -24.  Given that the Actual Expenditures of 2021 -22 and 2022 -23 
(till 31st January, 2023) are 89% and 62% of the allocat ed B.E. Estimates, the Committee 
feels that the Ministry should implement effective measures to optimally utilize the 
allocated resources.

21. The Committee notes that there has been a slight increase of Rs. 83.87 crores (5%) in the 
GBS at R.E. 2022-23 stage.  The increase was under the Capital outlay and the Revenue outlay 
was decreased by 15.08 crores. The increase, the first time in four years , is however under only 
three Heads, the Sagarmala Development Company (an increase of 100 crores in RE), Indian 
Maritime University (an increase of 62 crores in RE) and DGLL (an increase of about 20 crores 
in RE).  All other Budgetary Heads, barring two, have had their allocations reduced at  the 
Revised Estimates Stage. Despite this, the Committee notes that there has been considerable 
under-utilisation of funds across almost all the Budgetary Heads of the Ministry .  Though Rs. 
100 crores have been provided to the Sagarmala Development Company (SDCL), there has been 
no expenditure till 31.01.2023. The Committee notes that the reduction of fund s at RE stage 
definitely points to the inefficiency on the part of the Ministry in implementing various projects 
and inefficient utilization of budget allocation. 
22. The Committee notes till 31 st January, 2023, a total of Rs. 1154.17 crores have been 
spent against the Revised Estimates allocation of Rs. 1793.37, a utilisation percentage of

Coastal Shipping & IWT 
129. The MoPS&W, under its Sagarmala  Programme, has embarked on developing an 
ecosystem for promotion of Coastal Shipping and RORO/Ro-Pax Ferry waterway transportation 
in the country. This mode of transportation  has proved to have multiple benefits over other 
modes of transportation such as improved  cargo delivery and passenger travel time, reduced risk 
of accidents, improved operational speed, low-cost transportation, lower fuel consumption, lower 
congestion on roads and rail,  lowered air, noise and land pollution, along with providing 
seamless travel to passengers, and vehicles. 
130. To promote coastal shipping, Ministry  of Ports Shipping & Waterways has  undertaken 
following initiatives.  
 To encourage a modal shift, Coastal vessels are being provided  a discount of 40% in port 
charges over foreign going vessels.  
 reduction of GST on bunker fuel from l8% to 5%,  
 Cabotage relaxation for cargo vessels, integration of inland and coastal cargo. 
 Subsidy support to Indian shipping companies  
 Green channel clearance for coastal cargoes and priority berthing for coastal vessels at 
major ports  
131. Under the Sagarmala Programme, currentl y two Ro-Pax ferry services are operational  in 
the country on the Gogha- Hazira route in the state of Gujarat and Mumbai- Mandwa route in the 
state of Maharashtra bringing the travel time to 3 hours and 45 minutes with an  estimated carbon 
(CO2 emissions) reduction of 24MT per day and l3MT per day  respectively. These two services 
itself have benefited  more than 24.15 lakh  passengers and around 4.58 lakh passenger vehicles 
and 0.36 lakhs trucks till December 2022  and is continuously getting overwhelming pub lic 
response. 
132. Further, 9 projects including the above two have already been completed and  are 
expected to commence the services soon, and 35 more projects are under various stages of  
development and implementation. Moreover, dedicated berths for the movement of goods and  
passenger are being developed under the Coastal Berth Scheme. Five dedicated Coastal  Berths 
have already been constructed and another six are under development. 
133. Coastal Shipping is a competing mode for road and rail transport however with o nly less 
than 7% modal share of water transport.  India's transport modal share is relatively more skewed 
towards road and rail. Both road and rail transport are s ubsidised by various Government 
policies, however currently, no such benefit is available for the passenger and freight transport 
by Coastal Shipping i n order to reduce the burden on the operations of the Coastal/RORO/ Ro-
Pax ferry urban waterway transportation which are currently on the verge of unavailability due to 
above stated challenges/ issues and for augmenting this newly emerging ecosystem towards  
sustainable operations to compete with the copiously subsidised modes of transportation in  the 
country. Therefore in the Bu dget 2023 -24 to promote coastal shipping VGF guidelines  which 
shall be issued by Ministry of Finance will be followed to promote coastal shipping.

142. The efficiency of a port directly affects the economy of the country since the major share 
of the global trade is carried by sea . Ports handle around 90% of EXIM Cargo by volume and 
70% by value. During the pandemic, freight rates reached record highs. Surges in freight rates 
can affect the prices of goods and  impact global food security.  Ports are  therefore vital to the 
economy. 
143. Port performance indicators are measures of various aspects of a port‟s performance. 
Total cargo traffic handled and Turnaround time are good measures of a port‟s financial and 
operational productivity respectively. Turnaro und time is the total time spent by a vessel at the 
port from the time of its arrival to its departure. The Average Ship Berth Day Output (OSBD) is 
the total cargo handled by vessels/total stay at working berth.  
144. The Ministry has submitted that in order to meet the ever increasing trade requirements, 
expansion of Port Capacity has been accorded the highest priority through implementation of 
well-conceived infrastructure development projects. The government has given a strong push to 
port modernisation and d igitalisation, with a number of ease of doing business initiatives. 
National Logistics Portal - Marine has been developed to facilitate "Ease of Doing Business" by 
bringing all stakeholders (viz.,  Terminal operators, Shipping line agents, Banking, Exporters, 
Importers, Customs/Cargo clearing authorities, PGAs, logistics service providers etc.) onboard to 
enable seamless exchange of information/ documents in digital format through this portal. This 
Portal has been formally inaugurated by Hon‟ble Minister of P orts, Shipping & Waterways on 
27.01.2023. Direct Port Delivery and Direct Port Entry have been implemented in all Major 
Ports which has significantly reduced cost and dwell time.

158. The Ministry submitted that the following initiatives have been taken for the development 
and modernization of the Major Ports – 
159. Major Ports are shifting to the landlord model and increasingly going in for PPP 
partnerships.  Most of the assets are being given over through open competiti ve bidding to 
private partners for increasing efficie ncy and revenues of the ports.  JNPA has beco me the first 
port to adopt this landlord model fully.  For the operation part,  private parties are included to use 
the private sector efficiencies.  The other major initiatives for increasing port productivity are – 
 MPA Act 2021, enacted by the Parliament  in February 2021, will provide more 
autonomy to ports and help them take faster decisions in infrastructure development and 
changing market conditions 
 TAMP‟s role in the fixation of the tariff has been done away with in the new MPA Act, 
2021 as a tariff r egulator and ports would be free to set their tariff based on market 
forces.  
 The MPA Act, 2021 also provides for  the formulation of an Adjudicatory Board to 
adjudicate disputes among Major Ports, PPP concessionaires and captive use 
 SAROD Ports: To take ca re of the pending or future disputes between the ports and the 
concessionaires, the Society for Affordable Redressal of Disputes (SAROD -Ports) has

ANALYSIS OF PORT PERFORMANCE - Comparison of port capacity and 
performance with global standards 
The Committee appreciates the improvement in the port capacity, average 
Turnaround Time and Cargo Handling Capacity of major ports.  However, the Committee 
notes that the increase in Capacity and productivity still falls far short of International 
standards.  For instance, the Average Turnaround Time for all Ships has decreased only 
marginally from 52.80 hours in 2014 -15 to 50.01 hours in December, 2022. Only f or 
Container Ships the Turnaround time has decreased from 32.39 to 27.29 hours By contrast, 
the Turnaround time in Norway is only 10 hours. Singapore has 32 lakh TEUs per month 
and its port capacity is 65 lakh. In India it is only 8 lakh.  
(Para 156)

The Committee observes that none of India‟s major ports have as yet been ranked 
among the top 20 ports in the world on any performance index. India scores low on the 
Liner shipping bilateral connectivity index which aims at capturing a country‟s integration 
level into global liner shipping networks. A country‟s access to world markets depends 
largely on its transport connectivity. The turnaround time of the Major Ports of India has 
increased but still lags much behind the top international ports.  The Maritime India 
Vision 2030 aims to reduce dwell time and turnaround time to 40 hours and 20 hours 
respectively. The Committee asked the Ministry to give details about the plans for future 
growth in port performance to achieve the goals of Maritime India Vision 2030.  
(Para 157) 
DEVELOPMENT OF PORTS 
The Committee feels that since Port Development and Modernizations is highly 
capital intensive, efforts of both the Public and Private sector are the need of the hour. The 
Landlord Model of Port Development maximizes the efficiency of port operations. The 
Committee appreciates the other initiatives taken for port development. The Committee 
however feels that the policy of Land Management needs to be reviewed extensively as in 
the revised policy in 2014, the revisions were restricted to certain issues only.   
(Para 161) 
The Committee observes that the Vadhavan port with its natural draft of 20m is 
expected to handle large container ships of 16,000 -25,000 TEUs.  In comparison, JNPT 
presently the largest container handling maj or port has can handle only mid size container 
ships as it has a draft of 15 m whereas modern deep draft ports require a draft of 18 -20m. 
The Committee observes that the  size of Container ships  is increasing and it is very 
important to have a deep draft port to accommodate such ships. Moreover, Container 
traffic in the JNPT is expected to grow from 4.5 MTEUs currently to 10.1 MTEUs by 2022 -
25 when JNPT's potential will be fully exhausted. The Committee desires that the Ministry 
may make more efforts to de velop the Vadhavan Port rapidly as nearly two years have 
passed since the in principle approval of the port.

generation and add to the increased economic activity at other Indian Ports.  Among the

India a transshipment hub is a critical one. It will help India‟s maritime trade  to be cost

conduct business. In addition, critical vessel systems required for the safety of navigatio n, 
power supply and cargo management are increasingly digitized and connected to the 
Internet.  The Committee observes that digitalization is only going to increase manifold in

2. At the outs et, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the senior 
officers of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways to the meeting. The agenda of the 
meeting was deliberations on the Demands for Grants (2023 –24) of the Ministry. The Chairman 
noted that the B.E. allocations in 2023 -24 were significantly higher as compared to the 
allocations in the preceding three years and the increase was mainly in the Capital outlay. He 
sought to know the plans of the Ministry to utilise the enhanced Capital Outl ay. He   desired to 
know the performance of various schemes of the Ministry in both financial & physical terms. He 
also desired to know the reasons for slow progress under Port Modernization and the initiatives 
taken by the Ministry for promotion of coastal shipping mode of transportation.  
3. The Secretary informed the Committee that the Ministry has already attained an 
expenditure level of 75% in the allocations under R.E. 2022 -23. The Secretary then expounded 
on the major initiatives of the Ministry: 
 Promotion of Landlocked model of port development through PPP partnerships  at Major 
Ports 
 Development of Vadhavan Port in Maharashtra under the PPP model which is at the stage 
of environmental clearance 
 Development of International transhipment hub at Great Nico bar Island for which 
  Expression of Interest has been invited  
 Promotion of coastal shipping as an energy -efficient and low -cost mode of transport and 
increased cargo movement of 30 % on National Waterways in 2022. 
 Initiatives for promotion of Ease of doi ng business (EoDB)  including launching of a 
 single-window platform - National Logistics Portal -Maritime -   to enable end -to-end 
logistic solutions for maritime stakeholders for EoDB at ports, the promulgation of Major 
Ports Authorities Act, 2021, Marine  Navigation Act, 2021, Inland Vessels Act, 2021. 
 Other legislations like the Merchant Shipping Bill, the Indian Ports Bill and the Coastal 
Shipping Bill are expected to be introduced in Parliament shortly.   
 
4. Through his presentation, the Secretary briefed the Committee about the Gross Budgetary 
Support (GBS) and Internal & External Budgetary Resources (IEBR) Outlay of the Ministry. 
While the GBS for 2023 -24 was Rs. 2218.74 crores, the targeted Internal and Extra -Budgetary 
resources (IEBR) was Rs. 3633.21 crores.  The Secretary informed that the unique feature of the 
Ministry was that the IEBR was nearly 65% higher than the GBS. The ports were not being 
given any GBS but the Inland Waterways, still in a nascent stage of development, was dependent 
on GBS. Si milarly, Cochin Shipyard and Shipping Corporation of India were not given 
budgetary support except for R&D in case of Cochin Shipyard and specific programmes in case 
of the Shipping Corporation.  The Secretary also informed that while Cochin Shipyard and i ts

subsidiaries were under the Ministry, all other shipyards in India were under the Ministry of 
Defence. 
5. The Chairman queried about the reason the income of an independent, public limited 
company, the Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL) was being shown as the I EBR of the Ministry. 
The representatives of the Ministry stated that the revenue earned by the Corporation is being 
invested back in the projects of the Corporation. The Chairman stressed that the income of an 
independent company could not be included in t he budget of the Ministry under internal 
resources. 
6. The Ministry informed the Committee about its achievements in the port sector and the 
initiatives proposed for the FY 2023-24: 
 The capacity of major ports in the country has increased by 83% in the last s even years - 
from 871 Million Tonnes Per Annum (MTPA) in 2015-16 to 1597 MTPA in 2022-23; 
 The traffic handled at Major Ports during the period April, 2022 to January, 2023  
has increased by 9.31% in the FY 2022-23 on year-to-year basis. 
 Turnaround time for containers has reduced from 31.43 hours in 2017 -18 to 27.1 hours in 
  2022-23; 
 Average Output per Ship Berth day has improved to 17,026 tonnes in 2022-23. 
 52 PPP projects worth Rs. 37,200 Cr. have been completed and have contributed to the 
growth in port c apacity to the tune of 550 MTPA. 20 projects are under implementation 
and are expected to add 150 MT capacity.

 Efforts of all Major Ports to lessen the carbon footprint 
 Green Hydrogen Hubs to be developed at three major por ts, namely, Paradip, Kandla and 
Tuticorin; 
 20 PPP projects of Rs. 6,760 Cr. will be awarded

 Indo-Bangaldesh Protocol route (IBP) route cargo movement increased 51% from 3.58 
MMT in FY 2021-22 to 5.43 MMT in FY 2022-23 traffic; and 
 Under JalMarg Vikas Project in NW -1, Fifty one community jetties, five pairs of Ro -Ro 
terminals and modernization of existing Navigation Lock, Farakka are to be taken up   
 as well as awarding of O&M contract for Sahibganj and Varanasi MMT. 
  

99 
 
Proposed initiatives for 2023-24 
 The development objects for the next financial year, for the North -Eastern Region, are 
the Jogighopa Terminal; elevated road and ship repair facility construction at Mult i-Model 
Terminal, Pandu; cargo -cum-passenger terminal at Bogibeel, Dibrugarh; and fairway 
development. 
 O&M concessions will be awarded for Pandu Multi -Model Terminal and Dhubri Inter -
Model Terminal in the next financial year. Apart from that, Kareemganj an d Badarpur 
Terminal on National Waterway 16 will be upgraded and the Fairway Development will 
also be completed. 
Shipping sector 
 Cochin Shipyard Limited handed over Indigenous Aircraft Carrier (INS Vikrant) to Indian 
Navy on 28th July 2022; 
 The MoPS&W has setup India’s first National Centre of Excellence in Green Port & 
Shipping (NCoEGPS); and 
 CSL delivered two Autonomous/ unmanned Electric Vessels to M/s ASKO Maritime, 
Norway. 
Indian Maritime University 
 Admission for marine programmes 94% & overall admission 78% ; 
 New Courses for personnel operating Inland Vessels (under MIV 2030); 
 10 training programmes for Port Officials; 
 Implementation of e-Samarth (ERP) 
Directorate General of Shipping 
 Increase in number of employed seafarers by 21.5%   
 63 Indian Flag vessels added with addition of and 0.92 Million Gross Tonne added; 
 Number of digital certificate issued as on 31.12.2022 is 10,68,147; 
 Conduct of various grades of proficiency exam through remote proctoring; 
  Efforts to make all services electronic.  Capital expenditure is mainly towards IT purposes, 
system integration of the Directorate General and also construction of their buildings 
Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships 
 Two new Lighthouses constructed at  Kelshi (Maharastra) and Dhanushkodi (Ta mil Nadu) 
respectively; 
  
 

100 
 
Proposed initiatives for 2023-24 
 Two new Lighthouses at Rani Lakshmibai Shila (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) and 
Kalwan Reef (Gujarat) and recapitalization of Differential Global Positioning System 
Phase-II proposed in 2023-24; and 
 Promotion of Tourism at Lighthouses: Tourism development works at Gopnath Lighthouse 
completed while at Veraval and Dwarka Lighthouses to be completed by March 2023. 
 
9. The Committee was further informed that out of the pending 12 CAG Paras, only 3 Paras 
pertaining to Jawaharlal Nehru Port and the Vizag Port Authority are still pending against the 
Ministry as on 16.02.2023.   Action note for one Para has been uploaded on the Audit Para 
Monitoring System (APMS) portal. Action Notes for the remaining 2 Paras  will be uploaded as 
soon as the Regional Labour Commissioner and the Conciliation Settlement Committee   (CSC) 
give their awards 
10. A Member enquired about the green initiatives taken by the Ministry to reduce carbon 
emissions. The CMD of the Cochin Shipy ard briefed the Committee about the 23 fully electric 
hybrid buses for the Cochin Water Metro designed and engineered by the Cochin Shipyard and 
the fully battery powered KMLR vessels being delivered to a Norwegian supermarket chain. He 
informed about the Corporation’s work in development of India’s first hydrogen fuel cell vessel 
with the support of CSIR and a private Indian tech company, KPIT technologies. He further 
informed the Committee about contracts secured by the Corporation from German clients for  the 
construction of Construction Support Offshore Vessels (CSOV) to service off -shore wind power 
farm units, a milestone achievement in green energy. An MoU has been signed for production of 
all-electric vessels to be launched in four Indian cities. A Memorandum of Intent has been signed 
with a Norwegian company for the production of the world’s first hydrogen fuelled 
containerships. A National Centre for Excellence for Green Ports and Shipping has been set up at 
TERI campus in Gurgaon which will be the fulcrum for all of India’s green shipping initiatives. 
11. The representatives of the Ministry also informed the Committee about the green 
initiatives taken by the Major ports particularly Tuticorin port. Solar energy is a major initiative 
across all the por ts.  In Tuticorin, a 5MW ground based solar power project is ongoing along 
with a 2MW windmill project and a rooftop solar project,   all of which will make the port 100% 
green by the end of the year.   Another initiative is harnessing wind energy as certain  belts in 
India like Tuticorin and Kandla are very good for wind energy. This initiative is being carried 
out with the help of the National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) and the projects will be of 

101 
 
PPP model. The third major initiative is the Offshore Wi nd Programme in which studies are 
being conducted for exploiting offshore wind. Other green initiatives by ports include using 
LEDs, electric vehicles and electric cranes, production of green hydrogen, shore -to-ship power 
etc. 
12. A Member enquired about t he future plans of the Ministry in developing landlord port 
model on PPP basis.   The representatives of the Ministry informed that JNPA has become the 
first port to adopt the landlord model fully. Port is a sector where international competitiveness is 
needed and landlord model has the advantage of private sector efficiencies in the operations part. 
The landlord model is the way forward and most ports will follow this model. 
13. A Member enquired about the status of development of National Waterways NW -8, NW-
9, NW-13 and NW-59 and whether the DPRs have been shared with the State Government.  He 
emphasized that development of these Waterways should be on priority basis since they act as 
feeder routes to NW -3 which is also planned to be extended further.  A Me mber enquired 
whether the hundreds of ships plying below the Digha Bridge in Bihar were under the control of 
the Ministry. Another Member asked about the Ministry’s plans for development of Inland 
Waterways and whether any study had been done regarding Chi na’s transportation of cargo 
through its waterways.   The Member commented that the Ministry must make all efforts to 
promote waterways as this mode of transportation was the cheapest.  The Member suggested that 
if the GBS was not sufficient, the Ministry should think of the PPP model.  He also desired status 
on the Buckingham canal issue. 
14. The representatives of the Ministry informed that the NW -8, NW-9, NW-13 and NW-15 
waterways were notified in 2016 and the feasibility studies were conducted in 2019 an d shared 
with the State Government. Certain projects like construction of pontoon, dredging of waterways 
etc. have been taken up.   Issues relating to increasing the height of bridges and availability of 
land to keep the dredging material and terminals are being sorted out by the State Government 
for the development of waterways in Kerala.  Under the Inland Vessels Act, enacted in 2021, the 
control of survey, certification and registration is with the State Government. The vessels plying 
in the Digha Bridge have been registered with the State Government. Regarding the Ministry’s 
plans for Waterways, there is a Vision Plan of 2030 and a Vision Plan of 2047.   The long term 
plan is that the cargo has to increase to 200MT by 2030 which is expected to be achieved by 
2025 because in 2022, cargo of 109 MT has been achieved. Regarding the Buckingham canal, 

102 
 
the major issues are increasing the height of bridges and encroachments and the same have been 
taken up with the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. 
15. The Member also stated that Cochin Shipyard, a profitable PSU producing strategic ships 
should be promoted and should take up all Union and State Government projects wherever the 
Corporation is capable of providing vessels. Appreciating that the Corpo ration has delivered the 
indigenous Aircraft Carrier, INS Vikrant to the Indian Navy,    making India only the 6 th country 
in the world to design and build its own aircraft carrier, the Member stated that such profitable 
PSUs should not be disinvested.  Citing the example of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), 
another Navratna Company under strategic disinvestment, he commented that the scheme of 
arrangement for demerger of and transfer of non -core assets of SCI into another entity SCILAL 
(Shipping Corporation of India Land and Assets Limited) would countermine the Company.   He 
also raised the matter of non -payment of increments to seafarers despite a Kerala High Court 
order for setting up a tribunal on the issue. The representatives of the Ministry stated t hat the 
rationale behind disinvestment of a profitable PSU is the market interest and better value for the 
Government. 
16. A Member enquired whether the reduced budgetary support for Sagarmala was sufficient 
in view of the new projects proposed by the Mini stry.  He also enquired whether the Ministry 
would be financing projects under Sagarmala through PPP mode. The representatives of the 
Ministry informed that the schemes under Sagarmala are appraised every five years based on the 
expenditure made in the pre vious five years.   The expenditure was on the low side in 2019 -20 
due to Covid and also due to some issues in implementation of projects.   Therefore only Rs. 
1800 crore was allotted for the next five years which means Rs. 360 crores per year. The 
representative further informed that there are 55 under construction projects under Sagarmala 
and 51 projects under tendering. Money is released in three tranches, 50% at the time of award of 
tender, 40% upon completion of 50% physical progress and 10% upon complet ion of 100% 
physical progress. The representative also informed the Committee that with more than 100 
projects in the pipeline, the Ministry is confident of spending the budgetary estimates. Further, 
budgetary support is given only to those projects like c oastal community development which are 
not viable under PPP. Most projects of cargo handling in major ports are taken up under PPP 
mode. 
17. A Member suggested that the Central government should take up the cost of 
modernization and connectivity of non -major ports since it would not be possible for the State 

103 
 
Governments to invest huge outlays on such ports.   The Chairman also asked the Ministry about 
its plans for modernization of ports and the time span in which all major ports would be 
modernized. A Membe r asked about the increase in port capacity and whether the key 
achievements of Indian Ports in Turnaround Time, Ship berth day output etc. equalled 
international standards. The representatives of the Ministry submitted that the total capacity of all 
Major ports was 7,50,000 containers per month out of which 4,00,000 containers are being 
handled by the JNPT and 1,500 -1,800 containers by the Chennai port and rest by other ports. 
One Member pointed out that Singapore has 32 lakh TEUs per month and the capacit y is 65 lakh 
while India the capacity is only 8 lakh.   The Secretary replied that once Vadhavan port is 
developed, the port capacity of India would definitely increase. 
18. A Member asked whether a lighthouse was being constructed in Goa. The Chairman 
commented that lighthouses, being outdated technology, were basically being used for tourism 
purposes and enquired from the Ministry whether it was viable to invest crores of rupees in 
construction of lighthouses.    The representatives of the Ministry informed  that there are three 
lighthouses in Goa and proposal to construct more but the land falls under ASI.   The Ministry 
further informed that Directorate General of Lighthouses is a self -sustained organisation with its 
earnings mainly coming from charges levie d on container ships.   While lighthouses are one of 
the oldest technology based communication, the Ministry also has the latest advanced satellite 
technology including 23 DGPS stations and the biggest network of vessel traffic system.   
However lighthouses are also necessary since service to marine navigation is an international 
obligation for Government of India under IMO Convention. 
19. A Member raised the issue of stoppage of outer anchorage crew change at Vizhinjam port 
as significant revenue had been ea rned through the same.  The Committee was informed that the 
issue had been taken up with the Ministry of Home Affairs who had not agreed to the request and 
the State Government of Kerala had been informed of the same. The issues of crew change and 
customs clearance would be taken up if a fresh request is made. 
20. The Chairman commented that container manufacturing is very important but despite 
having the Container Corporation of India Company, India is presently dependent on container 
imports from China. T he representatives of the Ministry informed that manufacturing of 
containers is at a very nascent stage. The Ministry has drafted a PLI scheme for container 
manufacturing and the DG (Shipping) will be holding stakeholder consultations with the 
shipping sector. 

104 
 
21. The Chairman also enquired about the transshipment hubs planned by the Ministry 
especially the one in Great Nicobar island and commented that 75% of India’s transhipment 
cargo is presently handled at ports outside India, i.e. Singapore, Colombo an d Klang. The 
representative of the Ministry informed that Expression of Interest (EOI) has been floated for the 
transhipment hub and DPR is at draft stage. 
22. The Ministry was asked their plans for development of Andaman & Nicobar Islands to 
promote touri sm in that area. A Member enquired the Ministry’s plan of action regarding 
clearing the wrecked and rusted ships lying in the islands. 
23. A Member commented that the shipping industry creates many jobs for both skilled and 
unskilled people and asked whether the Ministry has a programme similar to the ‘Pradhan Mantri 
Kaushal Vikas Yojana’ (PMKVY).  
24. A Member also commented that there are 21 Dry Ports in the country but none within 
250 kms of Delhi.  The Member asked if the Ministry had any plans for Dry Ports near Delhi as 
it would be convenient to distribute containers from the port to inland. 
25. The Chairman also raised issues of cyber security in ports and the status of the six lane 
road project connecting Vishakhapatnam sea port to Bhogapuram airport  under Sagarmala.    He 
also enquired about the Polavaram dam project and how the Ministry proposes to ensure free 
passage of internal waterways ships while crossing the dam as the locks proposed in the dam 
were smaller.

BRIEF BACKGROUND 
An efficient, robust road network is a critical infrastructural requirement that enables the 
efficient movement of goods, people, and services across a region. It connects businesses to 
markets, workers to jobs, and people to vital services like healthcare and education. A well -
maintained road network can also help to reduce traffic congestion and improve safety, saving 
lives and time for commuters. The development of road networks has been shown to promote 
economic growth, as it fac ilitates trade and commerce, encourages investment, and boosts 
productivity. In rural areas, road networks can also connect isolated communities, providing 
access to critical resources and services. Overall, the importance of a well -connected, efficient 
road network cannot be overstated, as it plays a vital role in shaping the economic and social 
fabric of any society. 
2. India has the second largest road network in the world of about 63.32 lakh km. This 
comprises National Highways, Expressways, State Highw ays, Major District Roads, Other

Introduction and Mandate of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
3. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways was formed in 2009 by bifurcating the 
erstwhile Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways into two independent Ministries, 
i.e., Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and Ministry of Shipping. 


 
Page 2 of 137 
4. The tasks and responsibilities of the Ministry encompass, inter alia , construction and 
maintenance of National Highways (NHs); administration of the National Highways Act, 1956; 
National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988; National Highways Fee (Determination of 
Rates and Collection) Rules, 2008; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988; and Central Motor Vehicles Rules 
1989, a s also formulation of broad policies relating to road transport and automotive norms, 
besides making arrangements for the movement of vehicular traffic with neighbouring countries. 
5. The associated offices under the Ministry are as follows:- 
National Highways Authority of India 
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) was set up through an Act of 
Parliament, namely the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988. The NHAI is 
responsible for the development, maintenance and management of the Natio nal 
Highways entrusted to it and for matters related or incidental thereto. The NHAI became 
operational in February, 1995. 
National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corp. Ltd. (NHIDCL) 
The Cabinet, in its meeting held on 13 March, 2014, approved the s etting up and 
operationalization of a new corporate entity, the NHIDCL, under the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways to exclusively carry out the task of construction/up -
grading/widening of National Highways in parts of the country which share interna tional 
boundaries with neighbouring countries in order to promote regional connectivity on a 
sustainable basis. 
Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE)  
IAHE is a registered Society under the administrative control of the Ministry. It is a 
collaborative body that was set up in 1983 with the objective of fulfilling the long felt 
need for training of Highway Engineers in the country, both at the entry level and during 
their service period. 
Indian Roads Congress (IRC) 
IRC was formally registered as a Societ y on 24 September, 1937 under the Societies 
Registration Act of 1860 for the periodical holding of road conferences to discuss issues 
related to road construction, maintenance & development. IRC has over 16,850 registered 
members comprising engineers & pro fessionals of all stakeholders of the road sector, 
from Central and State Governments; Public Sector; Research Institutions; Academic 
Institutions; Local bodies; Private sector; Concessionaires; Contractors; Consultants; 
Equipment manufacturers; Machinery manufacturers; Material producers & suppliers; 
Industrial Associations; and Multilateral & Institutional organisations like World Bank, 
ADB, JICA, JRA, IRF etc.

National Highway Logistics Management Limited (NHLML)  
NHLML is a 100% owned subsidiary company  of NHAI. It is a Special Purpose Vehicle 
(SPV) company incorporated by the Ministry in the year 2020 with the intent of 
spearheading the development and inter -departmental coordination pertaining to the 
Multi-Modal Logistics Parks (MMLPs) for Cargo Traffi c and first/last mile Port 
Connectivity Road projects under the Bharatmala Pariyojana. NHLML has also been 
delegated by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for the development of other 
allied highway infrastructure such as Inter -modal Stations for passenger traffic and 
development operations and management of Way -side amenities along National 
Highways, Utility corridor along NH. NHLML has been pivotal in accelerating the pace 
of coordination with various State Governments and Partner Government Agen cies in 
terms of on -boarding them as equity stakeholders for development of MMLPs and 
signing of MoUs with various agencies. Since its inception, the organisation, under the 
supervision of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, has prioritised action on fast-
tracking first/last mile direct road connectivity for various major and non -major ports and 
Inland Waterway Terminals under Bharatmala Pariyojana, while coordinating with the 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and various Port agencies.

Rising Debt of NHAI 
77. On the issue of rising debt of NHAI, the Ministry informed that NHAI has been primarily 
assigned the mandate of implementation of Bharatmala Pariyojana during the year 2017. Prior to 
that NHAI was primarily executing projects under various phases of National Highways 
Development Projects (NHDP). In addition to the Government Budgetary Suppor t, NHAI has 
been raising debt from the market as per approved IEBR (Internal and Extra Budgetary 
Resources) to meet its target fund requirement as per the limits approved in the Union Budget. 
This resulted in increase in NHAI debt. Nevertheless, NHAI raise d funds judiciously as 
approved in Union Budget and with planned repayment options. 
78. Considering increase in debt service obligations of NHAI, the Government has not 
mandated NHAI to raise funds through market borrowings under IEBR since FY 2022 -23 and 
2023-24 and has provided additional budgetary outlay to bridge the gap. Thus, reduction in debt 
servicing liability has already started and as per present situation there shall be no further 
increase in the debt liability of NHAI at least till 31st March, 2024.  
79. NHAI is carrying out Asset Monetization programme for raising additional fund by 
monetizing its Road assets through TOT (Toll – Operate – Transfer) / InvIT (infrastructure 
Investment Trust) mode. NHAI is also carrying out securitization in the fo rm of SPVs (Special 
Purpose Vehicles) to raise the funds to minimize the debt and also to reduce the outstanding 
debt. One such SPV has already been formed exclusively for Delhi Mumbai Expressway. This 
will eliminate debt dependency of NHAI. 
80. The Minist ry has come out with several innovative funding mechanisms to increase 
private investments after 2014. During 2007 -14, private investments were confined to only BOT 
projects. Now, apart from BOT, HAM projects, we are also getting private investments throug h

Ministry has formulated a multi -pronged strategy to address the issue of r oad safety based on 
Education, Engineering (both of roads and vehicles), Enforcement and Emergency Care. 
Accordingly, various initiatives have been taken by the Ministry as detailed below: - 
(1)        Education:  
i.     To create effective public awarenes s about road safety, Ministry undertakes various 
publicity measures and awareness campaigns through social media, electronic media and print 
media. Further, Ministry implements a scheme to provide financial assistance to various agencies 
for administering Road Safety Advocacy. 
ii.    Observance of National Road Safety Month/Week every year for spreading awareness 
and strengthening road safety. 
iii.   A Certification Course for Road Safety Auditor has been mandated for technical officers 
of all road owning a gencies under the Ministry up to the level of Superintending Engineer or 
equivalent. 
iv.      To impart driving training, Ministry has been implementing a scheme for setting up of 
Institute of Driving Training & Research (IDTRs), Regional Driving Training Centres (RDTCs) 
and Driving Training Centres (DTCs) at state/district level across the Country. 
(2)  Engineering (both of Roads and vehicles) 
2.1. Road engineering: 
i.     Road safety has been made an integral part of road design at planning stage. Road 
Safety Audit (RSA) of all highway projects has been made mandatory at all stages. 
  
ii.    Road Safety Audit (RSA) of all National Highways (NHs) has been made mandatory 
through third party auditors/ experts at all stages i.e. design, construction, operation  and 
maintenance etc. 
  
iii.   High priority to identification and rectification of black spots /accident spots on 
National Highways. 
  
iv.   Road Safety Officer (RSO) has been designated at each Regional Office of road owning 
agencies under the Ministry t o look after RSA, blackspot rectification and other road safety 
related works. 
  
v.    Five stretches of NH having higher number of accidents/blackspots are being developed 
as Model Safe Roads under each regional office of all road owning agencies under the Ministry. 
  
vi.   Five project stretches under construction are being developed as Model Safe 
Construction Zones under each regional office of all road owning agencies under the Ministry. 
  

 
Page 121 of 137 
vii.     The electronic Detailed Accident Report (e -DAR) Project has been initiated to establish a 
central repository for reporting, management and analysis of road accidents data across the 
Country. 
  
viii.    Ministry and IRC has issued various codes and guidelines, time to time, to implement 
various road safety measures so as to minimize accidents on National Highways. 
  
2.2  Vehicle engineering: 
i.     The Ministry has notified regarding mandatory provision of an airbag for the passenger 
seated on the front seat of a vehicle, next to the driver. 
  
ii.    This Ministry, vide notification dated 15th February, 2022 has prescribed norms related 
to safety measures for children below four years of age, riding or being carried on a motor cycle. 
Further, it specifies use of a safety harness, crash helmet and restricts speed to 40kmph. 
  
iii.   Ministry has notified the mandatory fitment of following listed safety technologies from 
01st July 2019. 
For M1 category vehicles: 
a. Seat Belt Reminder (SBR) for driver and co-driver. 
b. Manual Override for central locking system 
c. Over speed warning system. 
For all M and N category vehicles: 
a. Reverse Parking Alert System 
  
iv. The Ministry has mandated Anti -Lock Braking System (ABS) for certain classes of L 
[Motor vehicle with less than four wheels and includes a Quadricycle], M [Mo tor vehicles with 
at least four wheels used for carrying passengers] and N [Motor vehicles with at least four 
wheels used for carrying goods which may also carry persons in addition to goods, subject to 
conditions stipulated in BIS standards] categories. 
        
v.    This Ministry has mandated approval of vehicles for protection of occupants in the 
event of an Offset Frontal Collision, for requirements for behavior of steering mechanism of the 
vehicle in a Head -on collision, Protection of Occupants in the event of Lateral Collision and for 
approval of vehicles with regard to protection of pedestrians and other vulnerable road users in 
the event of a collision with a motor vehicle. 
  
vi.   The Ministry has mandated speed limiting function/speed limiting device in all transport 
vehicles, except for two wheelers, three wheelers, quadricycles, fire tenders, ambulances and 
police vehicles. 
  
vii.   This Ministry has mandated compliance of the fully built buses (with a seating capacity of 
22 passengers or above, e xcluding driver), manufactured on and after 1st April 2019, with the 
requirements of Fire Detection, Alarm and Suppression system. Further, compliance of type III 
buses of category M3 and school buses with fire alarm and protection system in occupant 
compartment has also been mandated, on and after 26th January 2023.

viii.    The Ministry has prescribed the format in which vehicle manufacturers issue the Road 
Worthiness Certification for registering motor vehicles. 
  
ix.      Scheme for setting up one mod el Inspection & Certification Centre in each State/UT with 
Central assistance for testing the fitness of vehicles through an automated system. 
  
x.    Ministry vide Notifications dated 23 rd September, 2021 and 31 st October, 2022 
published the rules for recognition, regulation and control of Automated Testing Stations. 
  
xi.      Notification vide GSR 272(E) dated 05 th April. 2022, provides for mandatory fitness of 
vehicles only through an Automated Testing Stations.  It mandates the fitness check of Heavy 
Goods Vehicles/Heavy Passenger Motor Vehicles only through automated testing stations with 
effect from 01st April 2023 onwards, and for Medium Goods Vehicles/Medium Passenger Motor 
Vehicles and Light Motor vehicles (Transport) with effect from 01st June 2024 onwards. 
  
xii.     Ministry has formulated the Vehicle Scrapping Policy based on incentives/dis -incentives 
and for creating an ecosystem to phase out older, unfit polluting vehicles 
(3)        Enforcement: 
i.   The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 a s stands implemented provides for strict 
penalties for ensuring compliance and enhancing deterrence for violation of traffic rules and 
strict enforcement through use of technology. 
  
ii.   Ministry has issued notification G.S.R. 575(E) dated 11th August, 2 021 for Electronic 
Monitoring and Enforcement of Road Safety. The rules specify the detailed provisions for 
placement of electronic enforcement devices (speed camera, closed -circuit television camera, 
speed gun, body wearable camera, dashboard camera, Auto matic Number Plate Recognition 
(ANPR), weigh in machine (WIM) and any such other technology specified by the State 
Government).                          
(4)        Emergency care: 
i.     Ministry has published rules vide GSR 594(E) dated 29.09.2020 for the  protection of 
Good Samaritan, who in good faith, voluntarily and without expectation of any reward or 
compensation renders emergency medical or nonmedical care or assistance at the scene of an 
accident to the victim or transports such victim to the hospital. 
  
ii.    Ministry vide notification dated 25 th February, 2022 has enhanced compensation of 
victims of Hit and Run motor accidents (from Rs. 12,500 to Rs. 50,000 for grievous hurt and 
from Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 2,00,000 for death). 
  
iii.  The National Highways Authority of India has made provisions for ambulances with 
paramedical staff/Emergency Medical Technician/Nurse at toll plazas on the completed corridor 
of National Highways.

Road transport is a critical infrastructure for the economic development of a country. India has 
the second largest road net work in the world of about 62.16 lakh km. Evidently, the roads and 
highways are the life line of any country/region or an economy and the spin offs of such an 
activity results in all round economic development and GDP enhancement.  The resolve of the 
Ministry and its executing agencies is to give a thrust to infrastructure development besides 
protecting the environment by way of undertaking inclusive sustainable development will go in a 
long way in preserving and protecting our diverse eco-systems, protected areas, and eco-sensitive 
zones, fragile Himalayan, desert and coastal eco-systems etc. 
  
NHAI’s Sustainable Vision: 
The infra development and environment protection though are generally considered to be 
difficult tasks on the developmental canvas. Howeve r, taking this as a challenge, the Ministry 
and its executing agencies (i.e. NHAI, NHIDCL, State Govts., etc.), about 8 years back decided 
to proactively mainstream the tenets of sustainable development in its road network 
development.  This was quite a ma jor task for an organization wherein the main thrust is infra 
development to cover and connect all the major cities and habitation.  The vision of the Ministry 
is to develop eco -friendly NHs with participation of the community, farmers, NGOs, private 
sector, institutions, government agencies and the Forest Department for economic growth and 
development in a sustainable manner. This shows the commitment of an institution which is 
although infra centric yet it follows the principles of sustainable development and inter and intra-
generational equity.   
  
Sustainable Reporting: 
Sustainable development as we understand is an organizing principle for meeting human 
development goals while also sustaining the ability of natural systems to provide the natural 
resources and ecosystem services on which the economy and society depend. The desired result 
is a state of society where living conditions and resources are used to continue to meet human 
needs without undermining the integrity and sustainability of the natural s ystem. Moving in this 
direction, the NHAI is in a big way involving the Self Help Groups (SHGs), Non -governmental 
Organizations (NGOs) and especially the women for undertaking the various sustainable 
development initiatives.  
  
The NHAI is moving ahead to pursue the E.S.G. (Environment, Social and Governance)  
approach.  The NHAI is also now in the process of preparing “Sustainability Report” through an 
experienced and qualified Consultant ‘Deloitte’. This endeavor is going to be a periodic feature 
and would not only provide a much needed data base to review the qualitative and quantitative 
improvements in E.S.G. domain but would also be the beginning of a new chapter of 
environmental sustainability in NHAI .

Indian Road Congress (IRC) guidelines: 
The Ministry has adopted IRC guidelines, Standard Operating Procedure (SOPs) Expression of 
Interest (EOI) and Request for Proposal (RFP) to involve SHGs, NGOs, and private plantation 
agencies. Memorandum of Understanding (MoUs) arrangement is there in place to invo lve State 
Government Agencies- State Forest Department, State Forest Development Corporations, State 
Sericulture and Horticulture Departments. Further, NHAI is also contemplating involving 
industrial and corporate houses of repute which has a strong Corpor ate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) track record for CSR activities. The technical specification guidelines in the IRC were 
issued from time to time with regards to 2 -laning, 4 -laning, 6 -laning and express highways. 
These guidelines contain different provision s for raising and maintaining road side plantations, 
medians and landscaping etc.  The recent revisions are IRC SP: 73 which deals with 2 -lane 
highways (Year 2015 & 2018); the IRC SP: 84 which deals with 4 -lane highways (Year 2014 
and 2019); the IRC SP: 19 87 which deals with 6 -lane highways (Year 2013 and 2019) and the 
IRC SP: 1999 which specifically deals with the expressways, the revisions for which were 
affected in 2013, 2014 and 2019.  
  
Further, the IRC SP: 108 – Guidelines on Preparation and Implement ation of Environment 
Management Plan (EMP)  were notified in the year 2015.  This lays down comprehensive 
guidelines in conformity with the extant policies of the Ministry of Environment, Forests & 
Climate Change (MoEF&CC). It is mandatory to ensure complia nce to the stipulations of the 
IRC Special Publication IRC: SP: 108-2015 for all National Highways, Expressway projects, etc. 
in the project being implemented by MoRTH through its various implementation agencies. The 
provisions contained therein about mitigation of environmental damages are strictly applicable at 
all stages of projects. To keep pace with emerging international challenges and to meet its 
commitment to international conventions, vide IRC SP: 122 Guidelines on Reduction on Carbon 
Foot Print in  Road Construction Projects  was issued in 2019 for attending climate change 
aspects in road construction.

 INTRODUCTION 
2023 is the Incredible India! Visit India year and also the year of India‟s presidency of G20, 
presenting the perfect opportunity to establish India as a key tourism destination. This year 
therefore offers the brightest outlook for Indian tourism since the beginning of the pandemic in 
early 2020.   One of the largest Service Sectors in India, Tourism has always played a key role in 
socio-economic progress through employment generation, creation of infrastructure and revenue 
earnings.  Tourism also has the potential to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals, 
particularly, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, sustainable consumption and production 
and sustainable use of oceans and marine resources.  The huge potential of this key sector is set 
to be tapped further this year on Mission Mode with the active participation of states, the 
convergence of government programmes and public private partnerships.

15. The Committee observes that in the last three years, the allocation at the  Revised 
Estimates stage is half of the Budgetary Estimates and the Actual Expenditure is even less.  
The utilisation percentage of the Ministry for the last two years i.e.  2020-21 & 2021 -22 is 
only 89.85 & 82.89  respectively and for the FY 2022 -23 it is only 34.56% till 31 st January 
2023.While expenditure in 2020 may be understandably low due to the pandemic, the 
status in respect of 2021 and 2022 is no better.  The utilization percentage of only 34.6% in 
2022-23 is unacceptable.  The Committee does not accept the reply of the Ministry that the 
change in procedure of release of funds was a factor in low utilisation of funds. The change 
in procedure was for all Ministries and other Ministries have managed to utilis e most of 
their funds by December, 2022.   
16. The Committee finds that the reduction in Revised Estimates in the past three years 
is across all Central Sector Schemes. The Flagship Scheme of the Ministry, Swadesh  
Darshan has had budgetary cuts of upto 50%  at the Revised Estimates stage in the past 
three years. 
17. The Committee further finds that the entire budget allocation of Rs. 2400 crores is 
under Revenue Head with nil allocation to Capital Head.  The Ministry has submitted that 
a major portion of the  outlay amounting to Rs.1742 crores is earmarked for development 

Page 12 of 136 
 
of infrastructure for tourism development and Rs. 242.00 crores for promotion and 
branding activities.  For tourism infrastructure Schemes, an amount of Rs, 1412.00 crores 
is allocated for Sw adesh Darshan, Rs. 250.00 crores is kept for the Scheme of  PRASHAD 
(Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual and Heritage Augmentation Drive) and Rs 80 
crores is allocated for Scheme for Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism 
Infrastructure Development. 
18. Much of the budgetary outlay is for development of infrastructure. Swadesh  
Darshan, the flagship scheme of the Ministry is focused on development of theme based 
infrastructure. Infrastructure for all tourist amenities like creation of tourist information 
centre, reception centre, convention centres, cafeterias, beautification of tourist attractions 
are covered under this scheme.  The Committee does not find it rational that though 
Capital assets are being created unde r the schemes of the Minist ry, the entire expenditure 
is classified under Revenue.    Revenue expenditure is short -term, recurring expenditure 
mostly pertaining to salaries, operating expenses, administrative costs etc.  Due to its very 
nature, revenue expenditure cannot be reduced as the expenses such as salaries and wages 
are incurred irrespective of the activities carried out.  The Committee finds however that 
for the last five years, the budgetary allocation of the Ministry has been halved at the 
Revised Estimates stage and even this budget has remained unutilised.  The Actual 
expenditure for the past five years has been much less than the budget allocated in Revised 
Estimates. 
19. The Committee notes the submissions of the Ministry that though at the macro level, 
the budget is un der Revenue Head, yet within the Schemes, there would be Object Heads 
pertaining to “Creation of Capital assets.” Under the two Major schemes, Swadesh  
Darshan and PRASHAD, the re is no recurring expenditure on salary etc.  These schemes 
are mainly meant for  asset creation and only 5% funds are given for O&M (Operations 
and Maintenance).  However, though only assets are being created under these schemes, 
the outgo of funds can be reduced depending on the progress of the projects and receipt of 
Utilisation Certificates.   
20. The Committee observes that creation of capital assets leads to value creation and 
generates future cash flows for the economy.  Further, the multiplier effect of Capital 

Page 13 of 136 
 
expenditure is much more than that of the Revenue expenditure. In In dia, the multiplier 
effect of Capital expenditure made by the Central Government is estimated at 2.45 and for 
State Governments, it is around 2 while the multiplier effect of Revenue expenditure is only 
0.99 (RBI  Bulletin, December, 2 020) .  Wrong classif ication therefore may not give  the 
correct picture on total investment in infrastructure and may impact both the Index of 
Industrial Production and the GDP.  The Committee notes that the classification as 
Revenue is arbitrary without following any valid criteria in case of various projects of 
Ministry of Tourism. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up the 
matter with the Ministry of Finance and submit a detailed explanation to the Committee.
