42. Based on the detailed review, the Ministry has now revamped the scheme as Swadesh 
Darshan 2.0 (SD2.0) with the mantra of „vocal for local‟, and with the objective to develop 
sustainable and responsible destinations following a tourist & destination centric approach.  
Swadesh Darshan 2.0 is not an incremental change but a generational shift to evolve Swadesh  
Darshan Scheme as a holistic mission to develop sustainable and responsible to urism 
destinations covering tourism and allied infrastructure, tourism services, human capital 
development, destination management and promotion backed by policy and institutional reforms.  
The aim is to develop fewer locations but with a more visible and impactful development. The 
guidelines of the scheme include an illustrative list of admissible components and covers 
development of toilets, wayside amenities etc. at destinations. 
The key principles to be followed under Swadesh Darshan Scheme 2.0 are  
 (i) Develop benchmarks and standards for major tourism themes 
(ii) Sustainable and responsible tourism 
(iii) Destination and tourist-centric approach 
(iv) Integrated development of tourism destination 
(v) Focus on Domestic Tourism 
(vi) Policy and Institutional Reforms

geographical features, India offers something for everybody and is a Niche Tourism haven.

138. The Committee observes that the pandemic has changed not only the way we live 
and work but also the way we travel.  One of the major outcomes of the pandemic was the 
normalization of remote working which has given rise to the growing popularity of 
staycations, vacations in places nea r nature and remote places etc.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may take steps to conduct frequent market surveys and 
collect data to understand travel trends. The Committee observes that data and market 
intelligence surveys are vital for creat ing a road map for the travel industry as future 
travel is going to be very different.   
139. The Committee also observes that more tourism needs have evolved during the 
pandemic and Niche Tourism is one of the new trends post pandemic. Due to health and

generates future cash flows for the economy.  Further, the multiplier effect of Capital 
expenditure is much more than that of the Revenue expenditure. In India, the multiplier 
effect of Capital expenditure made by the Central Government is estimated at 2.45 and for 
State Governments, it is around 2 while the multiplier effect of Revenue expenditure is only 
0.99 (RBI  Bulletin, December, 2020) .  Wrong classification therefore may not give  the 
correct picture on total investment in infrastructure and may impact both the Index of 
Industrial Production and the GDP.  The Committee notes that the classification as 
Revenue is arbitrary without following any valid criteria in case of various proj ects of

matter with the Ministry of Finance and submit a detailed explanation to the Committee.

2. The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the witnesses who were 
present. The Chairman informed that the agenda of the meeting was to examine the Demands

for Grants (2023 -24) of the Ministry of Tourism. The Chairman noted that the budgetary 
allocation for Tourism sector was Rs. 2400 crores, i.e. the same as the allocation in 2022 -
23.  He further noted that the budgetary allocations in the past few years had been much 
reduced at the R.E. stage and that the utilisation percentage in the past two years was 89.85% 
and 82.89% respectively.   Out of the R.E. 2022 -23 allocation of Rs. 1343.13 crores, the 
Ministry has utilised only 34.56% till 31 st January 2023.  The Chairman wished to know the 
reasons why the Ministry was unable to utilize its allocated budget.  
 
3. The Chairman also desired to know the strategies formulated by the Ministry to 
harness India‟s presidency of the G20 to promote Indian tourism on Mission Mode and plans 
to utilise the funds allocated to Swadesh Darshan , the Ministry‟s flagship scheme.   The 
Chairman then highlighted some inaccuracies in statistics in Tourism Statistics for the years 
2021 and 2022 published by the Ministry and desired to know the methodology employed in 
measuring tourist footfalls in Indian states and monuments.  
 
4. The Secretary, the Ministry of Tourism acknowledged that issues regarding data 
collection were being faced as the data from state sources was not reliable.   To resolve this, 
the Ministry organises training in data collection to g round-level staff in states.   The 
Secretary stated that the issue would be looked into and training given to the staff in the 
concerned states. The Secretary then gave an overview of the Indian Tourism scenario – 
 International Tourists Arrivals (ITA) in India in 2021 were 7.01 million as compared to 
6.34 million in 2020, an increase of 10.6%.   
 Foreign Tourist Arrivals (FTA) numbered 61, 91,399 registering a growth of 305.4% 
over 15, 27,144 in 2021.  
 Foreign Exchange Earnings have also risen steadily from R s. 65,070 crore in 2021 to 
Rs. 1,34,543 crores in 2022, an increase of 106.8% over the previous year. Domestic 
tourism grew by 11.05% over the previous year 
 Tourism contribution to GDP in 2020 -21was 1.06% and to share of jobs in overall 
employment was 12.91% 
 
5. The Secretary briefed the Committee about the various offices/organisations under the 
administrative control of the Ministry and informed them that overseas tourism offices are 
being wound up and alternative methods would be used to promote tourism overseas. 
 
6. The Secretary then informed about the budgetary allocations under various Major 
Heads of the Ministry.   Elaborating on the major schemes of the Ministry, the Secretary 
informed that - 
 76 projects had been sanctioned for Rs. 5320.11 crores under its flagship scheme, 
Swadesh Darshan 1.0 out of which 59 have been completed. Progress in 14 projects is 
between 75% -99% and below 75% in the remaining 3 projects.   The scheme was 
implemented from 2014 -15 till 2018 -19. After review at the highest levels, i t was 
revamped in late 2022 as Swadesh Darshan 2.0 to focus on responsible and sustainable 
tourism by following destination centric approach instead of the earlier theme -based 
circuits. 48 destinations have been identified for development under Swadesh Dar shan 
2.0 through a consultative process with the State Governments.    No new projects had 
been undertaken while revamping the scheme and that was one of the reasons for the 
reduced allocations under Revised Estimates along with implementation -related 

140 
 
challenges. The Scheme has the largest budgetary allocation of Rs. 1412 crores this 
year.  
 PRASHAD Scheme aims at rejuvenating pilgrimage, heritage and spiritual experiences 
through well -developed infrastructure. Out of 45 approved projects in 25 states 
amounting to Rs. 1586.10 crores, 20 projects have been completed and progress in 9 
more projects is more than 60%. 250 crores have been allocated to this scheme this 
year. 
 Under the Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development 
Scheme, a total of 60 projects have been sanctioned for an amount of Rs. 841.08 crores 
and 22 projects have been completed till date. 80 crores have been allocated to this 
scheme this year. 
 Under the „Adopt a Heritage Scheme”, 27 MoUs had been awarded to 15 Monument 
Mitras who would take up the responsibility of developing tourist amenities at sites but 
the Scheme has now been transferred to M/o Culture/ASI.  
 Budgetary allocation of Rs. 75 crores has been made for Domestic Promotion and 
Publicity. Overseas Promotion and Publicity Scheme is under review.  
 Allocation of Rs. 70 crores has been done under the Central Financial Assistance for 
the 21 Institutes of Hospitality Management and Sciences and other institutes under the 
Ministry 
 A total of 1,04,371 persons have bee n trained since 2018 -19 till 30/11/2022 under the 
Scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers (CBSP) through Programmes such 
as Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, Skill Testing & Certification, Entrepreneurship Programme, 
Linguistic Tourist Facilitator, Adventure Tourism Courses, Destination Based Skilled 
Development Programme, etc. 
 An online digital platform to provide training and certification to tourist facilitators was 
launched on 1/1/2020.   IITTM is the implementing agency for this scheme and 4438 
candidates have completed the IITF Basic exam. 
 The Champion Services Sector Scheme has an allocation of Rs. 225 crores for 
extending incentives for improving Air Connectivity. In principle   approval has been 
accorded for 59 Air Tourism routes and 51 have been operati onalized. 140 crores have 
been allocated for the creation of tented accommodation in the Buddhist circuit and 90 
crores for Capacity Building in and around Iconic sites, 75 crores for Incentives to Tour 
Operators in Emerging Markets and 5.40 crores for the Promotion of MICE tourism.  
 The Iconic Destinations Scheme was not approved but some of the concepts have been 
incorporated in the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme.  
  The Incredible India website with 24 x 7 Live Chat support  interface and Mobile 
application co mprising of features like Maps,  Popular destinations, tourist attractions 
and experiences to assist tourists have been developed with content available in 
multiple foreign languages.  
 
7. A Member commented that none of the Members of the Committee were aware  that 
the Swadesh Darshan Scheme was being revamped and that 57 destinations had been selected 
after the revision of the Scheme. He enquired whether there had been any process of public 
participation or  consultation with Members of Parliament while prepar ing the guidelines for 
the revised Scheme. The representatives of the Ministry replied that State Governments were 
supposed to have public consultations before they submitted their proposals to the Ministry.

Members commented that the Schemes of the Ministry did not have any new components and 
appeared to be a rehash of the past Schemes.    
 
8. The Chairman commented that the Actual expenditure figure for 2022 -23 was very 
low at only 34.6% of the R.E. amount. He then enquired about the reason the entire budget 
allocation of the Ministry was shown in Revenue Expenditure only while infrastructure w as

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee observes that Souvenir shops selli ng miniatures of historical monuments 
are very popular among tourists in foreign countrie s. However, these sorts of souvenir shops are 
very scanty in India. The Committee would, therefor e, recommend that the Government ought to 
take initiatives to help establish genuine outlets for the sale of miniature replicas of historical 
monuments near such monuments. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 Under ‘Adopt a Heritage’ project, advanced amen ities are planned as per the identified 
monument’s tourist footfall and financial feasibility of proposed interventions. Provision of basic 
souvenir shop promoting local art and craftsmanship  is covered under advance amenities and 
may be implemented at the site upon adoption. It wo uld provide a platform to local 
artisans/craftsmen to sell their product and support the local community.  
 
1.2 The Ministry of Tourism has noted the recommend ation of the Committee. The Ministry 
will take up with the States to promote miniature s ouvenirs of historic monuments at various 
tourist destinations to create opportunities for the local community.

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that Prime Minister, Shri Na rendra Modi has mooted three 3-Ts -
 Trade, Tourism and Technology - to boost Indian ec onomic diplomacy and suggested that the 
functioning of Indian Missions and embassies should  be judged from their ability to inter alia 
boost tourist inflows. The Committee also takes not e of the submission made by Secretary (ER), 
Ministry of External Affairs before it that his Min istry will be closely working with the Ministry 
of Tourism to ensure greater progress in promotion of tourism and observes that apart from 
providing foreign exchange and mass employment, the  tourism sector has an economically 
beneficial cascading impact on other associated ind ustry segments and, therefore, the Ministry 
of External Affairs in coordination with the Minist ry of tourism and stakeholders needs to move 
quickly towards reworking India's strategy on attra cting foreign tourists to the country and help 
unleash the true potential of tourism sector in Ind ia. The Committee desires to be kept apprised 
of the progress made in this regard. The Committee also recommends that Indian Ambassadors 
as leaders of Indian Missions abroad must set targe ts for the growth of Indian tourism in key 
markets across the world with the objective of incr easing foreign tourist arrivals to the country 
and increasing the share of India in World Tourist Arrivals. The Committee desires to be kept 
apprised of the specific steps taken in this direction. 
(Para 45) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 It has been informed by the Ministry of Externa l Affairs that Indian Missions regularly 
organize events to promote culture and tourism. The se events include around Indian festivals, 
Indian products, performances with Indian/local art ists etc. Missions also regularly engage with 
the Tour Operators, in coordination with Indian Tourism Offices. 
 
1.2 Missions regularly organize quizzes related to India like ‘Bharat ko Jaaniye’ quizzes.

in India, their visits to pilgrimage centers and in viting distinguished guests under Gen next 
Democracy Programme, MEA plays an important role in promotion of tourism abroad.  
Likewise ICCR’s Cultural Centers and Chairs program me organize activities promoting Indian 
Culture which reflects every aspect of life.

Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes that only two Indian ports f eature in the top 40 Global Container 
Ports. It is obvious that there is significant pote ntial to develop port infrastructure in India and 
become competitive with other leading maritime nati ons by driving cost effectiveness. The 
Committee therefore recommends that overall capacit y augmentation of Indian ports should be 
done and cost competitiveness at Indian ports should be ensured in a manner that in the next 5-7 
years India has at least 5 of its ports by Container throughput in the top 40 ports. 
(Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 Suggestion of the Committee has been noted. How ever, it is informed that capacity 
enhancement at Major Ports is a continuous process.  The Government is regularly monitoring 
the Port projects for development/expansion of the Major Ports. Port Projects such as 
construction of berths, installation of state-of-th e-art equipment, mechanization of cargo 
handling system and dredging projects to accommodat e large size vessels, etc. help in increasing 
the Capacity of Major ports. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee also notes that the Ministry of Po rts, Shipping and Waterways had 
informed that as compared to the full capacity of t he major ports of 2,500 million metric tonnes, 
the total volume of cargo that was moved on all our  major ports was about 1,248 million metric 
tonnes. The Committee was informed that this was du e to the fact that most of India's ports were 
pretty old with less draft and old berths due to which big ships can not come in. The Indian Ports 
therefore have adequate capacity but there is a nee d to modernize them so that they are able to 
handle cargo on a larger scale. 
(Para 20)

Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 Maritime transport activity is driven by develo pments in the world economy - growth in 
world output and trade. The volume of seaborne carg o traffic handled by ports is mainly shaped 
by the levels and changes in both global and domestic activity. 
2.2 The Sagarmala Programme, the flagship programme  of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & 
Waterways lays great emphasis on modernization and mechanization. Ports are looking at setting 
up specialized high-capacity berths, supported by s tate-of-the-art equipment and skilled and 
trained manpower. 
2.3 To develop global standard ports in India, Mari time India Vision (MIV) 2030 has

Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee observes that the success of a por t project can be ensured only if careful 
planning is made at the formulation stage itself re garding evacuation and connectivity by 
involving Railway Authorities/ NHAI etc., addressin g all technical aspects. The Committee 
emphasizes that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways, waterways etc. should be 
part of the infrastructure planning process right f rom inception stage. Approach to a port from 
the hinterland can be critical enough to make or ma r a Terminal because it determines the 
turnaround time and evacuation time - vital to the functioning of a port. Evacuation is a vital 
component of any port project as the capacity and e fficiency of the port vitally depend on the 
rate at which the cargo can be evacuated from the t erminal. The efficiency, viability and 
business depend on how well connected the port is. The Committee therefore recommends that 
the measures to be taken for the connectivity of a port to the roads and railway networks, to 
airports, to service roads connecting nearby towns and villages should be an essential 
component of the project from its formulation stage itself and be a part of the Detailed Appraisal 
Report so that the integrated infrastructure can be  developed with proper connectivity and 
interlinking. Despite the enormous importance of th e connectivity of ports, the Committee feels 

Page 24 of 48 
 
that the pace of work under this head has been even  slower than that under modernization of 
ports since out of 208 projects only 56 have been c ompleted and 69 are under implementation. 
Out of the 1.36 lakh Crores funding under this head , only a paltry sum of Rs. 19,488 Crores has 
been utilized till date in completed projects. The Committee also notes that there appear to be 
very few connectivity projects relating to minor po rts. The Committee notes that the MMLPs 
planned at strategic locations in the country would  bring down logistics costs and boost the 
national economy. The parks will enable the shift f rom a point-to-point to a hub-and-spoke 
model in the logistics sector, eventually helping t o bring down logistics costs by at least half and 
enabling more efficient movement of new-generation vehicles. The Committee however is 
constrained to note that actual work has commenced in only one of the MMLPs at Jogighopa in 
Assam with construction of the Phase-I expected to be finished by December, 2023. In two 
MMLPs at Nagpur and Chennai, MoUs have been signed for development, in only six MMLPs 
land has been identified for development while pre- feasibility studies are still going on in the 
remaining MMLPs. The importance of a modern and eff icient logistics network can not be 
overemphasized. Poor connectivity across various lo gistic modes not only increases the wear 
and tear of transport means and damages to goods, b ut also leads to uncertainty in supply 
chains leading to further decrease in the route uti lization by trade and thus, increasing rates for 
the remaining users. Sagarmala aims at construction  of wider roads for connectivity of Ports to 
another point. However, unfortunately, the Committe e noticed that in some cases the Sagarmala 
Projects are undertaken only upto major cross roads  on the route and thereafter no effort is 
made to construct road upto “Point” envisaged in the Sagarmala Project. The Committee has no 
hesitation to point out that in such a situation the wider roads/ connectivity between the Port and 
the POINT envisaged in the Sagarmala Project beyond  the point of cross roads will remain 
unfulfilled. The Committee, therefore, recommends t hat the “point to point” Sagarmala 
connectivity envisaged may be implemented irrespect ive of the fact that there exist major cross 
roads in between. The Committee stresses that road connectivity under Sagarmala should not be 
only point to point but encompass the entire periph eral network of roadways interlinking nearby 
towns, villages, service roads, important tourist p laces, national monuments etc. for the overall 
development of the areas. The Committee emphasizes that service roads should be included in 
the DPR itself, and given as much importance and be  developed to the same quality as regular 
roads.

that was moved on all major ports was 1,248 million  metric tonnes in 2020. Though the 
Government has taken a number of initiatives to mod ernize our ports under the Sagarmala 
Programme, a lot remains to be done to ensure deep-draft availability to handle mega-ships. The 
Committee observes that increased competition and e conomy of scale has fueled the 
development of bigger ships and to accommodate such  vessels, ports must have access channels 
of sufficient depth along with advanced and highly efficient terminal facilities. The Committee 
observes that the drafts at major ports, both in th e channel and berths, have been historically 
low and ranges from 7 meters in older ports up to 2 0 meters in newer ports and is not

to their respective cargo profile The Committee is of the considered view that dredging, which 
can increase the draft in ports, is a must for deve lopment of port-led industrialization. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that there is an urgent need to increase the draft of almost all 
the ports of the country under the Sagarmala Progra mme, for which, the requirement of

11. The Committee notes that dredging comprises cap ital dredging and maintenance 
dredging. Capital dredging is done to either create  new channels, basins, berths, etc. or to 
deepen the existing such infrastructure. Such dredg ing is highly capital intensive. Presently, 
most of the ports in India are meeting their expend iture towards maintenance and capital 
dredging through their internal resources. The Comm ittee has been informed that dredging 
constitutes a major portion of total project cost a s well as operating cost and if it is funded 
through internal resources and borrowings, it entai ls an increase in overall port cost and 
consequently tariff. The Committee has also been in formed by stakeholders that one of the 
reasons behind high Vessels Related Charges (VRC) i n India is the inclusion of dredging cost in 
computation of tariff and that is why Indian ports are touted as high cost ports. The Committee 
has further been informed by the stakeholders that the concept of full cost recovery from direct 
users/ beneficiaries is not followed in Canada, Jap an and most West European countries. 
Internationally, and especially in developed countries, port channels are used as a national asset 
and dredging projects are funded by local municipal ities or Governments, and not by ports 
themselves. One of the most comprehensive legislati ons on cost sharing in dredging is the US 
Water Resources Development Act, 1987 under which t he Federal Government meets 50% to 
90% of the dredging costs. Similarly, dredging is t he responsibility of the National Government 
at Colombo. Taking into account the above fact, the  Committee recommends that the 
Government should explore the possibility of treati ng the channels as a national asset and 
funding the entire dredging cost. The Committee wou ld also like the Ministry to study different 
practices in other countries for funding dredging, both capital and maintenance, and formulate a 
funding mechanism in respect of Indian ports.

Consequential Train Accidents  
Recommendation/Observation

accidents from 2010-11 to 2022-23. The Committee al so congratulates the RDSO for the

way in reducing accidents through a cost-effective measure. The Committee recommends that 
KAVACH should be introduced phase-wise, through all  the routes of India Railways. In first 
phase, all the routes where there are regular cases  of accidents should be considered and 
KAVACH should be installed expeditiously. 
(Para 41)

1.1. As informed by Ministry of Railways, 
i. Till now, 1445 Route km of Indian Railways netwo rk in South Central Railway has been 
brought under Kavach. 
ii. Kavach roll out is being planned in a phased ma nner as below: 
a. At present Kavach roll out is planned on 3000 Ro ute km of New Delhi – Mumbai and 
New Delhi – Howrah routes for which tendering is in  progress and finalized for 1165 
Route km.  
b. Further survey and detailed estimate preparation  for 6000 Route km on balance 
GD/GQ Route is in progress. 
c. Subsequently Kavach will be provided on other Routes of Indian Railways.

Role of the Ministry of Civil Aviation  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the Deputy Commissioner s of Railway Safety come from 
Ministry of Railways on deputation basis and go bac k to the Ministry after completion of their 
deputation period. The Committee notes that the Deputy CRS is one of the senior most officers in 
the circle offices and comes second in hierarchy af ter the CRS. The Committee feels that such an 
important post should not be filled up on deputatio n basis, as the incumbent may not be inclined 
to give suggestions/ recommendations in his Reports  against the Ministry of Railways, to which 
he originally belongs and would be sent back after his deputation period is over. The Committee 
recommends that the officers of the rank of Deputy CRS should be appointed in the Commission 
on absorption basis, just like the CRS and it should not be a deputation post. The Committee is of 
the firm view that appointing Deputy CRS on absorption basis will ensure grant of full autonomy 
which would make the Commission more independent and effective. 
 (Para 17) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 As per Recruitment Rules of the post of Dy. CRS , the officers are equivalent to Director 
rank officer i.e. level-13 whereas CRSs are of Addi tional Secretary rank officer i.e. Level-15, 
which are recruited on absorption basis from amongs t Railway Officers with minimum 05 years 
service in Level 14. Hence, if Dy. CRSs are selecte d on permanent absorption basis in the 
Commission under Ministry of Civil Aviation, there will hardly be any promotion avenue for 
Dy.CRS. Hence, existing system of taking officers on deputation seems adequate. 
 
Upgradation of post of CCRS and requirement of sepa rate Secretariat for

Role of the Ministry of Civil Aviation  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that presently the powers of  the CRS are derived from the Railways 
Act, 1989. The Committee also notes that in exercise of the powers conferred under the Railways 
Act, 1989, the Statutory Investigation into Railway  Accidents Rules, 1998 are framed by the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Railway (Notices  of and Inquiries into Accidents) Rules, 1998 
are framed by the Ministry of Railways. Further tho ugh the CRS functions under the 
administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviatio n, the Commissioners of Railway Safety are 
recruited from amongst officers of Indian Railways on absorption basis and the Deputy CRS 
work in the Commission on deputation basis. The Com mittee also notes that the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation provides administrative, establishment and  financial support to the CRS. The 
Committee is of the opinion that the involvement of  two Ministries viz, Ministry of Railway and 
Civil Aviation, leads to avoidable confusion in the command structure of the CRS and there is an 
urgent need to free the CRS from the undue influences of both the Ministries. 
 (Para 16) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Commission of Railway Safety is an independent apex statutory body on the matters 
pertaining to Safety of Indian Railways and Metro R ailways. To have adequate effectiveness of 
the Commission as an independent agency, Ministry o f Civil Aviation is of the view that 
autonomy of Commission of Railway Safety needs to b e maintained by way of consultation by 
Ministry of Railways with the Commission while maki ng changes in those chapters of Indian 
Railways Act/Manuals etc. which pertain to Commission’s working. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.2 The Committee desires to know the specific step s taken by the Ministry or the plans 
thereof to ensure the functioning of the Commission  as an independent agency and free 
from any influences of both Ministry of Railways an d Ministry of Civil Aviation. The

be made in relevant Acts/Rules/Manuals, to maintain  the autonomy of the Commission of

3. The Committee notes that as per the existing sch eme, the Ministry of Railways have full 
power and authority to amend the provisions of the Railways Act, 1989. However, the Committee 
notes with serious concern that Ministry of Railway s brings about unilateral change in such 
rules, codes and manuals, without consulting the CR S which has a bearing on jurisdiction of the 
Commissioners. The Committee also notes that the Railways Act, 1989 also gives absolute power 
to Ministry of Railways in accepting/regulating/mod ifying any condition proposed by CRS. The 
Committee notes that the CRS is the Principal Techn ical Advisor to the Ministry of Railways, in 
safety related matters and is of the firm opinion t hat the views of the CRS should mandatorily be 
taken into account in such cases. The Committee the refore recommends that the Ministry of 
Railways should avoid unilateral changes in Rules, Codes & Manuals which affects Railway 
Safety without consulting CRS. If any, changes are made it should be based on consensus 
between Ministry of Railway; Ministry of Civil Avia tion and the CRS. The Committee also 
recommends that a complete review of the procedure adopted for amending provisions in the 
Railways Act, 1989 may be done to include the suggestions of CRS.  
(Para 24)

3.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation is of the view that autonomy of Commission of Railway

Report 
 India has always been one of the richest countries in the world in terms of archaeological and 
cultural wealth but the protection of this rich cultural herit age has always posed a challenge . In 
medieval times, invaders like Nadir Shah carried off a great many priceless gems and jewels and 
ancient fabled treasures. Under British colonial rule, there was a systematic and rapacious looting of 
India’s treasures. British museums today are filled with priceless antiques from India like the 
Sultanganj Bud dha, Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s throne and the sword and rings of Tipu Sultan. The 
looting of India’s treasures did not stop with independence from colonial rule but the heritage theft in 
the post-independence era has not gained as much prominence and visibility.   
2. While the colonial plunder of India’s tangible cultural heritage is well known, the 
contemporary rampant theft and smuggling of countless idols, antiquities and artefacts from the 
temples, forts, archaeological sites and even museums in modern In dia has gone largely unheeded.  
Many of these incidents of heritage theft are often not reported to the law enforcement agencies or to 
the ASI, possibly because no one knows exactly what has been stolen and when it has been stolen. 
As per UNESCO estimates, about 50,000 idols and artefacts had been stolen out of India till 1989. 
Despite various measures taken by the Government to curb smuggling of the Indian cultural wealth, 
many challenges still prevail in the process of  documentation, identification, safe guarding and 
repatriation of antiquities and lost cultural wealth.  
3. Cognizant of the massive scale of looting of our priceless antiquities, the Committee decided 
to take up the subject ‘Heritage Theft – The Illegal Trade in Indian Antiquities and challe nges of 
retrieving and safeguarding our Tangible Cultural Heritage’. The Ministry of Culture and its attached 
office of the Archaeological Survey of India are the nodal organisations concerned with the 
preservation and conservation of antiquities, but the humongous volume of our cultural wealth 
spread throughout the country and the sheer scale of theft of antiquities taking place means that the 
exercise of preservation of our cultural treasures requires the involvement of many government 
departments, NGOs a nd civil society organisations. The Committee , therefore, heard the Ministries 
of Culture, Home Affairs, External Affairs; Archaeological Survey of India (ASI); Directorate of 
Enforcement (ED); Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI); Central Board of In direct Taxes and 
Customs (CBIC); Idol Wing of the Tamil Nadu Police; and Indian National Trust for Art and 
Cultural Heritage (INTACH) in its meetings held on 15 th November, 2022; 25 th November, 2022; 
22nd December, 2022; and 5th January, 2023.

I 
Documentation of Tangible Cultural Heritage 
4. The Ministry of Culture informed the Committee that documentation of antiquities plays a 
very vital role in retrieving or claiming the stolen antiquities and proving the ownership of the said 
antiquity. India has a vast heritage and cultural repositories that are scattered all over the country. 
Some are protected by ASI, some are under state government and some are under Trusts/ local 
authority/ private ownership, etc. A big chunk of movable heritage is unprote cted and scattered all 
over the country without any vigilance and protection. While theft of antiquities in the Centrally 
Protected Monuments/sites under ASI and under State Governments is immediately reported and FIR 
is lodged, theft of unprotected antiquities which are neither documented nor reported makes retrieval 
of stolen property very difficult. The documentation of all such antiquities in the form of digitized 
records alongwith maintenance and periodic auditing of inventory is the first step to ensu re the 
safeguarding of India’s tangible cultural heritage. In this regard, the Government had launched a 
National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (NMMA) to document the country’s monuments 
and antiquities which will help in creating a database of all antiquities and can be referred to readily 
in case of fraudulent dealings or theft in antiquities. 
 
National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities 
5. The National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (NMMA) was launched on 19 th March, 
2007 for an initial pe riod of 5 years from 2007 to 2012. It was extended for a further period of 5 
years till 2017 and was later merged with Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). The objectives of 
NMMA are as follows: 
 Documentation and creation of suitable database on built her itage and sites through published 
and unpublished secondary sources for information and dissemination to planners, researchers, 
etc. and for better management of such cultural resources. 
 Documentation in a uniform manner developed by NMMA, of all Antiquiti es that are available 
in different formats in the form of Registered Antiquities, Catalogued Antiquities with Central as 
well as State Governments, Private museums and Collections, Universities, etc. 

Page 3 of 108 
 
 Promote awareness and sensitize people concerning the be nefits of preserving the historical and 
cultural aspects of built heritage, sites and antiquities. 
 Extend training facility and capacity building to the concerned State Departments, Local bodies, 
NGOs, Universities, Museums, Local communities etc. Help in developing synergy between 
Archaeological Survey of India, State Departments, concerned Institutions and NGOs to 
generate close interaction. 
6. Through inputs from eminent scholars, researchers, heritage  professionals and bureaucracy, 
the NMMA has develope d 21 parameters for cataloguing antiquities/sculptures and artefacts. These 
21 parameters are comprehensive and uniform in nature and have been approved by the Ministry of 
Culture. Till date, NMMA has documented 16.8 lakh antiquities out of 58 lakh antiqui ties, which is 
approximately 30 percent of the total estimated antiquities. Out of this, 15.7 lakh antiquities were 
documented by the NMMA before its merger with the ASI. This database also contains information 
of antiquities which are in the custody of the Archaeological Survey of India. 
7. The Ministry informed that any person can access 12.28 lakh templates of antiquities already 
published on the NMMA website. However, there are 3.5 lakh templates of antiquities, in possession 
of private individuals, which have been documented by NMMA, which cannot be accessed by the 
general public as per the guidance of the Ministry of Law. These remaining templates can be 
accessed by State Governments, law enforcement agencies, Non -Governmental Organisations 
(NGOs) and private museums, with special permission from the Competent Authority. 
8. The Ministry further informed the Committee that in most of the museums, the objects on 
display is a small fraction of what is there in the reserve collection.  The Ministry is al so considering 
the items kept in the reserve collection for the digitization process. There is a rotation policy in the 
Museums wherein objects are replaced from reserve collection to display from time to time, for the 
benefit of visitors/scholars, etc. 
9. The Committee notes that in the 15 years since  the inception of NMMA, only about 16.8 
lakh antiquities out of a total estimated 58 lakh antiquities i.e. about 30% have been 
documented as on date. Further,  the Committee was informed by  DG, ASI in the deposition 
that the figure of 58 lakh antiquities is only an estimate and there may well be many more 
antiquities existing in India. If so, it makes the slow pace of documentation un der NMMA all 
the more alarming.

Risk Management System (RMS) 
90. The Risk Management System (RMS) con sistently aims to strike a balance between trade 
facilitation and Customs interdictions. It aims to support the field officers in effective decision 
making by providing them with all the relevant information regarding an incoming or outgoing 
consignment. E valuation of consignments is done by using a host of risk parameters which are 
continuously evolved by using local, national and international risk trends, offence databases and 
feedbacks from the field received. Only the consignments deemed risky on any of the evolved factors 
are sent to the field officers for Assessment or Examination purposes. On the basis of the analysis of 
the self -declaration made by importer/exporter, Shipping Lines, Vessels involved, various risk 
factors are identified. The paramete rs are determined utilizing details such as the countries/ports 
involved; exporter/importer involved; consignee/supplier involved; commodities declared; Import 
General Manifest (IGM)/ Export General Manifest (EGM) declarations; past behaviour of entities 
involved etc.

smuggling like smuggling of Red Sanders; Antique goods; Narcotics Drugs & Psychotropic

are under the joint copyright of the French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP) and the French

Annexure-V 
Modus Operandi adopted for Smuggling of Antiquities 
The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) informed the Committee that the Directorate is investigating a 
number of cases related to smuggling/theft of Art and Antiquities objects under the provisions of 
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. The investigation conducted by the Directorate 
of Enforcement has revealed following modus operandi adopted by the accused persons:- 
Modus Operandi-1 where buyer is the mastermind 
In these types of cases, the antique smugglers first select a temple to carry out thef t/stealing antique 
idols of Hindu deities. Then, they visit the temple site to ascertain the timings, dates, crowding at the 
temple etc. They also enquire from people living around the vicinity of the targeted temples and try 
to gather details of antique i dols which were kept in the temples. After getting these details, the date 
for stealing of the antique idols is decided. The theft is carried out in the night. After theft the antique 
idols are transported from that place to the person (broker) who is hand ling all the activities on 
behalf of the Mastermind Smuggler sitting outside India. The broker gives some money in cash, to 
all the participants of the theft as a commission and keep all the antique idols. 
Thereafter, the broker, who is the owner of an art  gallery, fabricates the letterhead of another art 
gallery as if the stolen idols are newly made handicrafts items and attempts to export the same to the 
mastermind in a foreign country by approaching Handicrafts Department to obtain a Certificate for 
newly made handicrafts. The stolen idols are mixed or replaced with the newly made handicrafts 
items subsequently. The Certificate obtained from the Handicrafts Department is produced before the 
Customs Authority at the time of exporting the stolen idols to th e mastermind. After receiving the 
idols, the mastermind sends commission money to the broker who is in India in his bank accounts in 
the guise of payment made towards the purchase of Handicrafts items. The mastermind sells these 
antique idols in the intern ational market at exorbitant rates and acquires illegal money. The value of 
the smuggled antique idols is estimated to be in several crores in the international market. 
Modus Operandi-2 where buyer is identified after execution of theft 
In these cases, the  accused first steals the antiquities from the unknown historical places, 
archaeological excavation sites, ancient temples etc. Then, the stolen antiquity is taken to another 
place till the buyer is found and deal is materialized. After receipt of desired amount, the antiquities 
are smuggled/exported in the guise of exportable goods to the address of buyer. In one of the cases, 

Page 102 of 108 
 
the accused tried to ship the antiquities through courier in the form of ‘Brass Hindu four handed lord 
Vishnu statue’ and ‘Vintage brass tobacco weighing scale’ before being apprehended. In other case, 
the accused was apprehended with the unknown antiquity in his possession. The accused was 
searching for a buyer for the antiquity for an amount of Rs. 5 crore.

Details of Subhash Kapoor case  
 
Subhash Kapoor, a US citizen and owner of New York based Art Gallery - Art of the Past was found to 
be the mastermind behind smuggling of a large number of Antiques from India.  
 An intelligence was passed on by DRI to its overseas officer in New York on 14.02.2007 
regarding smuggling of antiquities in a shipment that was declared to contain “Garden Tea Sets” 
in the shipping bill presented in India. The said shipment was exported by “ Palace Knit Exports, 
Ludhiana” to “Nimbus Import Export Inc., NY”.  
 The said intelligence was shared by the overseas officer in New York with the officers of US 
Customs and Border Protection (CBP). 
  The shipment was, however, declared to US Customs as cont aining antiquities (in addition to 
items like marble tables). The importer had declared these items as antiquities pertaining to the 
period 2nd Century to 19th Century and valued at USD 60,400, in the invoice dated 05.01.2007.  
 The shipment of seven wooden  crates was detained and later examined by US Customs in the 
presence of overseas officer at New York on 22.02.2007 and it was found to contain, inter alia, 
various idols/figurines (mostly of metals). The Indian exporter and CHA denied having exported 
the consignment. The telephone number given on one of the import documents in USA was 
found to belong to “Art of the Past Inc.” (website: www.artofpast.com), a company located in 
New York, dealing in Asian antiquities and owned by Mr. Subhash Kapoor.  
 The examined antiquities were seized by US CBP and they conducted follow up. 
Simultaneously, surveillance and searches were also carried out by DRI in India on various 
exporters around the country, suspected to have links with smuggling of antiques.  
 A cla im was lodged in New York with the US Customs & Border Protection (CBP) for 
restitution of the seized Indian antiquities in August 2007.  
  Investigations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) of the U.S.A searched various galleries and 
warehouses owned/controlled by Mr. Subash Kapoor in USA on 5th January 2012 and recovered 
more than 2000 antiquities, valued at more than Rs. 1000 Crore. Some of these were of Indian 
origin. It was further revealed that he had supplied a number of antiquities to various US Art 
Galleries/ Museums/Private collectors. In cooperation with US enforcement agencies, these were 
recovered from time to time.

Additional District Magistrate, Kumbakonam, Tamil Nadu.  
The US Department of Justice sought access to Subhash Kapoo r through a request under Mutual Legal

Legal/ Constitutional Position of Retrieval of Antiquities taken out of the Country prior to 
Independence   
Article 253 of the Constitution of India reads as under: 
“ Legislation for giving effect to international agreements.- 
 Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power 
to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any 
treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at 
any international conference, association or other body” 
Section 166A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is as follows: 
“Letter of request competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India. 
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Code, if, in the course of an investigation into 
an offence, an application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank 
to the investigating officer that evidence may be available in a country or place outside India, 
any Criminal Court may issue a letter of request to a Court or an authority in that country or 
place competent to deal with such request to examine orally any person supposed to be 
acquainted with the facts and circumstances o f the case and to record his statement made in 
the course of such examination and also to require such person or any other person to 
produce any document or thing which may be in his possession pertaining to the case and to 
forward all the evidence so taken or collected or the authenticated copies thereof or the thing 
so collected to the Court issuing such letter. 
(2) The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as the Central Government may 
specify in this behalf. 
(3) Every statement recorded or document or thing received under sub - section (1) shall be 
deemed to be the evidence collected during the course of investigation under this Chapter.

the meeting.  The Chairman queried from the Ministry about the number of incidents of 
theft/loss of ancient antiquities/ sculptures/ artefacts which have occurred in  the last decade, 
the mechanism in place to safeguard the antiquities and the lacuna existing in the same. He 
asked the Ministry to brief the Committee about the coordination mechanisms employed by 
the Ministry with the Ministries of Home Affairs and Exter nal Affairs, and the Directorate of 
Revenue Intelligence in recovery of the stolen artefacts and the efficacy of the existing 
legislations/ rules/ regulations and mechanisms to recover the lost and retrieved art and 
antiquities. He also asked the Ministry to apprise the Committee of the reasons for non -
maintenance of an integrated database for stolen antiquities coming under purview of 
Central/State Governments and private organisations. 
  
7. Thereafter, the Chairman asked the DG, ASI, Head, Central Antiqui ty Collection and 
DG, National Museum, New Delhi, to inform the Committee about the existing mechanisms 
regarding physical verification of the artefacts lying in the Museums/Collections under their 
purview and whether the security personnel and arrangement s in place to ensure the safety of 
the artefacts are sufficient as per the requirements of such museums. 
  
8. Referring to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)’s   2022 ‘Report on 
the Performance Audit of Preservation and Conservation of Monuments and 
Antiquities’which was a Follow Up Report on its 2013 Report on the same subject and which 

118 
 
contained concerning observations on persisting issues such as acute shortage of staff, lack of 
digitization and accession of artefacts, their display, verification, conservation, storage and 
security, etc. the Chairman queried about the protracted delay in resolutio n of issues first 
raised by the CAG nine years before in 2013.  
 
9. The Chairman also queried about the status of the proposed amendment to the 
Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, reasons for slow progress in registering only 16 lakh 
out of 58 lakh od d-antiquities by the NMMA, efficacy of the Act in meeting modern 
standards, reasons for rejection of CSR funding by ASI, the budget allocated to it and 
requirements and shortfalls arising in carrying out its mandated activities, the number of ASI 
sites in India that require repairing and maintenance and the reasons for delays thereof, and, 
reasons for negative image of ASI among the general public. 
  
10. The Secretary, M/o Culture informed the Committee that the mandate of the Ministry 
is to preserve, prote ct and disseminate Indian culture within and outside the country and the 
mandate of its attached subordinate office, the ASI, is to preserve the ancient monuments of 
India and showcase them as tourist sites. The Secretary acknowledged that the subject of 
heritage theft also came under the ASI which implements the Antiquities and Art Treasures 
Act (AAT) 1972 to regulate the internal trade in antiquities/art treasures and prevent 
smuggling/ export/ fraudulent dealing of antiquities and art treasures. The Comm ittee was 
also informed about the compulsory acquisition of antiquities under the AAT Act and 
mandatory requirement of registration of certain classes of antiquities after notification by the 
government. The ASI, however, admitted that compulsory acquisiti on of antiquities had 
never been done and that the rate of registration, at about Rs 3 to 5 lakhs, was very low due to 
concern among citizens about the consequences of registration. However, ASI was spreading 
awareness about the importance of registration,  and ways of making the registration process 
simpler were being explored. 
  
11. The Committee was informed that legislation, security and retrieval were the 
processes through which Government tries to prevent heritage theft and illegal trade of Indian 
antiquities. Ancient Monuments & Archaeological Sites & Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958 
was modified to authorize the government to issue a notice prohibiting the removal or 
transportation of antiquities from places of their specific locations and punish violators with a 
jail term. Also, ASI communicates/ consults with other nations to bring ba ck smuggled 

119 
 
Indian antiquities from foreign countries under the 1970 United Nations Convention, which 
prohibits and prevents the illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property 
and which was ratified by India in 1972. ASI apprised the  Committee of the challenges faced 
by it in retrieval and safeguarding Indian tangible/cultural heritage, art and antiquities, such 
as, lack of coordination on part of State Govts and law -enforcement agencies, lack of 
awareness about antiquity documentation, lack of documented database of Indian antiquities, 
distrust and fear among people in case of mandatory antiquity registration, need for a more 
convenient/reliable antiquity registration system, etc.. 
  
12. The ASI informed the Committee that cognizant o f the need to document all antiques 
in the country, including those with private persons/institutions, the Government had, in 
2007, started a National Mission for Monuments and Antiquities. Out of an estimated 54 lakh 
antiquities in the country, this Mission had so far documented 16.7 lakh antiquities, including 
3.52 lakh antiquities which are registered antiquities. The ASI had also initiated 
documentation of its 52 site museums which contain all the excavated material. This  process 
is expected to be completed by the end of 2023. 
  
13.       The Committee was informed that keeping antiquities secure and tracking them in 
case of theft is much easier in monuments under Central Government as round the clock 
security, watch & ward staff, state police and Centr al Industrial Security Force (CISF) have 
been deployed in the monuments/museums under preventive measures. In such cases, FIR is 
lodged immediately and a “Look Out” Notice is issued through the CBI and all the Custom 
exit channels are alerted. In the case of State protected monuments, FIR is generally lodged 
but the relevant information does  not come to the ASI. Tracing and retrieval of antiquities 
which are unprotected or under private ownership is the most challenging as in case of theft, 
they are mostly reported as general theft and the information generally is neither reported to 
the State Government or the ASI. Also, the ASI has interactions with and conducts training 
programmes for various investigative agencies including CBI and customs authorities an d 
from time to time to sensitize their employees about heritage loss.  ASI officials are also 
deputed from time to time to conduct joint or surprise checks to curb fraudulent dealing of 
antiquities, check stocks of different dealers etc. Besides, in case o f suspicious consignments 
in the major customs channels of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Jodhpur and Thiruvananthapuram, 
Archaeological officers are deputed to examine such objects along with Customs Officials. 
These efforts have resulted in reduction in number of thefts and higher rate of  recovery of 

120 
 
stolen antiquities. Once the objects are held, they become “Case Property” and kept in police 
custody till the case is settled, upon which they are returned to the owner and if the owner is 
not known, they are confi scated by ASI and then generally stored in the Central Antiquity 
Collection, Purana Qila.   
  
14.       The Committee was informed that 229 antiquities have been repatriated from abroad 
between the years 2014 to 2022 as compared to only 13 from 1976 upto 2 014. The process of 
retrieval involves the MEA which plays a key role in negotiations with the foreign 
authorities. However, foreign museums are reluctant to return Indian antiquities despite 
availability of documents/evidence and often took recourse to th eir domestic laws which 
prohibit the export of any antiquity. Thus, use of international fora was necessary for 
consensus among nations for the retrieval of stolen heritage.  It was informed that the 
restitution of cultural property was one of the importan t items on the agenda of the Ministry 
of Culture for the upcoming G20 summit to be presided over by India. ASI was also working 
on the possibility of foreign museums at least acknowledging the provenance of Indian 
antiquities in their possession, even if the objects are not returned to India. 
  
15.       The Committee was informed about the thriving business of selling fake antiques 
which are difficult to identify without detailed scientific analysis. The Ministry also   apprised 
the Committee of its antiqui ty digitization software - ‘JATAN’ through which every item of 
the five National Museums are proposed to be digitized.  On the query regarding preservation 
of oral/intangible heritage of North -Eastern India,  Ministry informed that as an active 
member of th e UNESCO 2003 Convention, it has included 14 inscriptions of intangible 
cultural heritage and also has 165 current research items. Besides, the Sangeet Natak 
Akademi, an autonomous body under the Ministry also works towards preserving and 
promoting the rich Indian intangible cultural heritage. 
  
16.       Regarding a Member’s queries on doing base valuation for retrieved antiquities and 
the registered antiquities of the country to enable   more awareness  of the significance of our 
historical assets as our n ational wealth, and, statutory provisions for self -declaration by the 
erstwhile royal families and big business houses of antiquities they own so that the antiquities 
are not lost between generations,  the ASI informed the Committee that it will take neces sary 
steps to do base valuation of retrieved antiquities. The Committee was informed that the 
royal families are not keen on self -declaring their assets with the govt.  Chairman then 

121 
 
enquired whether Government can be given a preemptive right if a family w anted to sell an 
antiquity.   Regarding the query about whether there was any intelligence system to track 
auction at large auction houses to check on the sale of Indian antiquities, and country wise 
lists of disputed antiquities, the   ASI informed that th ere is no formal system but acquiesced 
to the suggestion of the Member that there should be an intelligence system tracking the 
interface to get prior intimation of the auctions. There was no country wise list of stolen 
antiquities, but the ASI was also at tempting to document the known cases of stolen 
antiquities at least among the G20 nations.  
 
17.       Making an observation on the slow progress of documentation of antiquities, the 
Chairman wanted to know whether the registration of antiquities which are  privately owned 
can be made mandatory and whether amendments were needed to be brought in the AAT 
Act, 1972 to meet the current situation. The Director -General, ASI admitted that registration 
process should be made simpler and unexacting before making it mandatory. It was felt that 
the statutory provisions of the AAT Act, 1972 were adequate but the implementation by the 
State Governments is inadequate. 
  
18.       Regarding the Chairman’s query on bringing back Kohinoor Diamond, the Ministry 
informed the Committee that Kohinoor was taken long before the AAT Act, 1972 came into 
effect, and was therefore not covered under the current legal framework of India. The matter 
can be pursued only through bilateral negotiations by the Ministry of External Affairs. AS I 
and Ministry confirmed that the AAT Act had only prospective effect to which the Chairman 
suggested exploring the possibilities of retrospective effect in this regard. 
  
19.       A Member also expressed concern on the dilapidated conditions of the India n 
Museum, Kolkata, the first Museum in India and enquired about the technologies used in 
digitization, the security arrangements in place, and the storage and preservation of artifacts, 
the Ministry apprised the Committee that the Museum is re -curating nine galleries and there 
is a plan of complete overhaul of the museum.   Regarding the dilapidated condition of the 
Bibi ka Makbara, Aurangabad, Maharashtra, ASI informed that due to the ancient structure 
and resource crunch, it is impossible to restore it fully. 
  
20.   Members also  raised queries on issues such as protection and preservation of 
archaeological sites located in the Tiger Reserves in coordination with National Tiger 

122 
 
Conservation Authority (NTCA), possibility of having a barter exchange of antiq uities with 
countries asking for their antiquities from India, status of fossils in antiquities, lack of 
CCTV/surveillance system and proper lighting around the Museums/archaeological sites, 
recovery of the remaining 119 antiquities out of the 210 stolen, status of the Nobel Prize 
Medal of Guru Rabindranath Tagore stolen from the VisvaBharati University, rules and 
procedure of selling private antiquity collection and buried treasure troves,  technologies used 
in digitization as well as digital archival of documented records, provision for basic amenities 
and eateries near forts for tourists, recruitment of staff in ASI offices to tackle manpower 
shortage, amenities, lighting and information centre at Anchuthengu Fort 
Thiruvananthapuram, repair work at Kannur Fort under ASI to protect the dilapidated 
monument, filling of vacancies in Thrissur Circle office, dismal state of Gagron Fort under 
State Archaeology in Jhalawar, fake antique collections, employing online auction tracking 
system to prevent online smuggling of antiquities,  etc. 
  
21.       The Chairman directed that written replies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week. 
 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
 
(The Committee re–assembled after lunch break)

2.         At the outset, the Chairman extended a warm welcome to the Members of the 
Committee.  He informed them of the agenda for the meeting i.e. (i) to consider and adopt the 
draft Reports on Action Taken by the Government on t he Recommendations/Observations of 
the Committee contained in its 317 th and 318th Reports; and (ii) to hear the representatives of 
Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs (CBIC); Director General, Directorate of 
Revenue Intelligence (DRI); and Director o f Enforcement, Enforcement Directorate (ED) on 
the subject ‘Heritage Theft – The Illegal Trade in Indian Antiquities and the challenges of 
retrieving and safeguarding our Tangible Cultural Heritage’. 
3.         The Committee, thereafter, took up the first agenda of the meeting i.e., consideration 
of the two draft Action Taken Reports on the following Reports of the Committee: 
(i) 317th Report on Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways; and 
(ii) 318th Report on Demands for Grants (2022-23) of Ministry of Tourism.  
4.         The Committee considered the said draft Reports and after a brief discussion, adopted 
both the draft Action Taken Reports and authorized the Chairman to carry out minor 
modifications of typographical and factual errors.   
5.         The Committee also authorized Shri Jugalsinh Lokhandwala, M.P. and in his absence, 
Shri Mohammed Nadimul Haque, M.P., to present the abovementioned Reports in Rajya 

125 
 
Sabha on 23 rd December, 2022 and Shri Prince Raj, M.P. and in his absence, Shri Ramdas 
Chandrabhanji Tadas, M.P. to lay the Reports on the Table of Lok Sabha on the same date. 
6.         Thereafter, the Chairman welcomed the Director, Enforcement Directorate (ED);  
Special Secretary & Member, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC); 
Director General, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI); and other senior officials of the 
agencies to the meeting. He enquired from the agencies details of the role played by them in 
prevention of smuggling, and retrieving and safeguarding of antiquities. He so ught to know 
their views on the existing legislation/Acts/Rules to curb theft and smuggling of antiquities 
and the changes needed to be incorporated into the existing laws. He asked CBIC and DRI to 
share their views on the efficacy of the existing customs export procedures in tracking and 
prevention of smuggling of antiquities in the country and the loopholes therein. He further 
sought to know about the steps taken to ensure better coordination amongst CBIC, DRI, ED, 
Ministry of Culture, Archaeological Surv ey of India (ASI), State Police agencies and various 
other State Government law enforcing agencies to curb the theft and smuggling of antiquities 
at the State level itself. 
7.         Director, Enforcement Directorate informed the Committee that the smuggl ing of art 
and antiquities is an offence under the Antiquities and Art Treasures (AAT) Act and under 
various provisions of the IPC. He apprised the Committee that ED has two Acts – the 
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and the Foreign Exchange Mana gement Act 
(FEMA). He stated that the ED registers a case under the PMLA as soon as there is an FIR 
with regard to smuggling of antiquities and there is predicate offence.   He informed that the 
focus of ED is to identify the proceeds of crime and that any person who has dealt with the 
proceeds of crime is dealt with under the provisions of the PMLA. He apprised the 
Committee about the various powers of ED under the PMLA, to seize the proceeds, 
investigate the accused, file a chargesheet upon completion of t he investigation, request the 
competent court to issue letter of request to other countries for obtaining information, for 
collecting evidence from other countries, to request the country concerned to freeze, seize, 
confiscate, and repatriate the assets, a nd for extradition of the accused if they have left the 
country after committing an offence under the PMLA. He further informed that under FEMA, 
ED can levy penalty and, in certain circumstances, attach the proceeds of crime in case 
somebody has parked mon ey which is generated from smuggling of antiquities, outside the 
country. 

126 
 
8.         Director, ED apprised the Committee that ED is investigating a couple of cases under 
the PMLA wherein the amount involved in a particular case pertaining to Tamil Nadu is 
nearly Rs. 800 crores, and that though the middleman in that case has been examined by ED, 
it could not arrest the accused because proceedings cannot be initiated under PMLA against a 
person extradited from a country by an agency not involved in the extrad ition proceedings 
unless and until the competent court in that country permits the same. He stated that 
nowadays both the agencies like CBI and ED jointly go for extradition proceedings to avoid 
facing the problems faced in this case. He informed the Commi ttee that under PMLA, all the 
categories of people involved in the cases of theft and smuggling of antiquity can be 
prosecuted – the person or gang involved in stealing of antiquities, the person involved in 
their sale, the person involved in their smuggli ng, the main kingpin who mostly resides 
outside the country and the person who purchases it. Briefing the Committee about the 
methodology for inter-agency coordination, he informed the Committee that the Customs and 
DRI file a prosecution complaint under S ection 208 of Criminal Procedure Code, on receipt 
of which, ED registers the case under the PMLA. He further stated that the Central Economic 
Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), a Central agency, coordinates among all the agencies. He further 
elaborated that under the provisions of PMLA, ED has sufficient power for the coordination 
and dissemination of information, for example, to the Law Enforcement Agency concerned, 
who is duty-bound to register the case. 
9.         Special Secretary & Member, CBIC informed the C ommittee that CBIC’s role as 
regards antiquities starts when the antiquities are being exported out of India. He stated that 
given a large number of passengers travelling out of India every year and the huge volume of 
trade from India, Customs authorities cannot check each consignment and/ or passenger as it 
would be against ‘Ease of Doing Business’ norms and the larger policy of facilitation of 
cargo exports. He stated that in case of passengers, the main check exercise is from the 
security perspective, with a minimal check of check -in baggage of passengers. He added that 
CBIC uses technological tools by way of advance passenger information system, applies a 
risk-based approach and identifies passengers who may be suspicious for a thorough 
checking. With re gard to cargo, he stated that CBIC employs risk -based management 
approach, which uses artificial intelligence machine -learning tools for identification of cargo 
which may be considered as risky for thorough examination. He informed that less than 10 
percent cargo is subjected to examination at the time of export and that there is possibility of 
concealing items given such large flow of cargo from the country. He stated that on receipt of 
intimation from State police/ ASI or any other authority regarding any  stolen antique, an alert 

127 
 
circular is issued to all customs formations to keep a watch. With regard to coordination with 
other agencies, he informed of forums like CEIB at the Central level and Regional Economic 
Intelligence Committees (REICs) at the State  level. He apprised the Committee about a case 
where Customs, using its channels abroad, informed the U.S. Customs administration about a 
consignment that went out of India, based on which the United States (U.S.) Customs and 
Border Protection agency inter cepted the consignment when it reached U.S. on basis of the 
information passed on by the DRI. 
10.       Special Secretary & Member, CBIC further informed the Committee that AAT 
provides for application of the Customs Act in relation to all antiquities and art treasures, 
allowing CBIC to seize such consignments at the time of export and that as per AAT, the 
determination of whether a suspected item is antique or not is done by a competent officer of 
ASI. He stated that the restitution of stolen antiquities c an be ensured only if the theft has 
already been reported in INTERPOL and it is duly registered. He briefed the Committee 
about two cases of antiquity theft that were detected/ prevented by DRI in the last five years.  
11.       Director General, Directora te of Revenue Intelligence apprised the Committee that 
DRI draws powers from the Customs Act and deals with anti -smuggling work, drug 
trafficking cases and customs duty evasion cases. He informed that the penalty prescribed 
under the Customs Act is three t imes the value of the goods and there is a provision for 
imprisonment of six months to three years, and up to seven years of imprisonment in case of 
repeat offences. He stated that the penal provisions take care of the deterrent effect for such 
crimes. He informed the Committee that DRI does passenger profiling in case of passenger 
movement and employs the techniques of getting the scanning inputs from the security 
agencies at the airports. He added that DRI applies risk parameters to the export 
consignments in the containers and has procedures of collection of intelligence to detect cases 
of smuggling. He stated that the wide definition of antiquities in the AAT Act poses a 
practical problem as the official who has intercepted an item cannot ascertain wheth er the 
item is antique or not. He further added that DRI coordinates with all other intelligence 
agencies and sources available within India and outside and has overseas officers posted in 
the Missions abroad, and these Missions, with the help of the Minis try of External Affairs, 
have been bringing the antiquities which had been seized abroad back to the country. 
12.       Members raised various queries regarding steps taken to curb smuggling of items 
across Bihar -Nepal border, possible measures for profili ng/identification of new persons 
involved in smuggling of antiquities based on risk analysis, restitution of seized antiquities to 

128 
 
respective temples or museums, tracking of illegally exported Indian antiquities being 
auctioned by auction houses, using art ificial intelligence and robotic technology for better 
checking of cargos to curb smuggling of antiquities, valuation of antiquities, list of stolen 
antiquities that have went out of India, trafficking of drugs through Gujarat and Maharashtra 
borders, details of antiquities missing from 12 missing monuments in Delhi, low conviction 
rate under PMLA, inadequacy of manpower available with CBIC at Kochi airport, tackling 
the issue of display of fake antiquities in private galleries and museums, number of Indian  
antiquities brought back to India out of the 2000 antiquities seized by the Investigations and 
Customs Enforcement (ICE) of the U.S.A, feasibility of a barter system to exchange 
antiquities belonging to other nations and compulsory installation of CCTV ca meras at 
archaeological sites and temples, etc. 
13.       On the query raised by one of the Members regarding low conviction rate under 
PMLA, Director, ED replied that their conviction rate is 95.2%. He added that 1,100 cases 
are on trial but in a large nu mber of cases the prosecution is pending because the police has 
not filed a chargesheet. He further informed the Committee that ED has attached the proceeds 
of crimes of Rs. 1,05,000 crores out of which, in four cases, assets of Rs. 15,000 crores have 
been returned to the banks. He apprised the Committee about the problem faced in valuation 
of antiques as there is no standard method of valuation of antiques in the economic sense and 
that ASI follows its own methodology of valuation of antiques and paintings . Citing his 
experience of valuation of antiques as an erstwhile Member of Tirumala Tirupati 
Devasthanam, the Chairman stressed upon the need for a methodology for valuation of 
antiquities by the appropriate agencies which would be useful in case some untoward incident 
happens.  
14.       Special Secretary & Member, CBIC briefed the Committee about the process of 
checks performed by CBIC on containers to be exported. He stated that Customs allowed 
self-sealing of containers in their premises, so the exporter seals the goods in a container with 
an electronic seal and Customs just checks the integrity of the seal,  thus more than 90 
percent of such containers are exported without examination by Customs. Based on the Risk 
Management System, CBIC examines some co ntainers, which strikes a balance between 
enforcement and facilitation. Responding to some of the issues raised by the Member, he 
shared that Customs is aware of the challenges of the Indo -Nepal border and has a number of 
land Customs stations for the bord er. He also informed the Committee about the repatriation 
of seven artefacts from Glasgow Museum, United Kingdom (UK) and a stolen 10 th century 

129 
 
Goat-headed Yogini’s sculpture to the High Commission of India, UK through the efforts of 
overseas Customs Officers of India. He further stated that the recruitment of  Group ‘B’ level 
non-gazetted officials  is presently done through Staff Selection Commission which takes a 
cycle of two to three years and that the  issue of lack of manpower can be tackled if the time 
period for recruitment can be shortened. 
15.       The Chairman directed that written replies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week. 
 (The witnesses then withdrew)

INITIATIVES UNDERTAKEN BY MOPS&W TO EXPEDITE IMPLEMENTATION OF 
PORT CONNECTIVITY PROJECTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the various Ministries to expedite the 
implementation of the Port Connectivity Projects. It also notes that the Ministry of Road 
Transport & Highways and NHAI has also carried out a detaile d prioritization exercise and 
had shortlisted 38 road connectivity projects which are at DPR stage and likely to be 
awarded by the F.Y. 2022. The Committee is of the opinion that such a capital -intensive 
infrastructure project which seeks to improve port, rail and road connectivity involving 
various ministries, State Governments can be successful, only if all the concerned agencies 
give utmost attention to the time bound completion of the portion of work allocated to each 
one and maintain close coordination  cooperation amongst themselves. The Committee hopes 
that all out efforts would be made by all the stakeholders to complete the work allocated 
within the time schedule. The Committee also desires to know the status of the award of work 
relating to the 38 road connectivity projects and the percentage of work completed. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 NHAI, in their report dated 04.03.2021, had prioritized 38 port -road connectivity 
projects which are at different stages of DPR and planned for award by FY22. 
1.2 However, after the latest exercise of Comprehensive Port Connectivity Plan (CPCP) 
prepared by DPIIT and shared in September 2022, 55 port road connectivity projects under 
MoRTH were prioritized. The status of these projects as shared by MoRTH is giv en in 
Annexure-1. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee further notes that a SPV under NHAI viz. National Highways 
Logistics Management Ltd. (NHLML) has been incorporated in 2020 to develop Multimodal 

Page 3 of 53 
 
Logistic Parks (MMLPs) and works related to National Highways connectivity to ports. The 
Committee is of the firm opinion that the MMLPs is a step in the right direction and such 
parks, if planned at strategic locations in the country would bring down logistics costs and 
boost the national economy. The parks will enable the shift from a point -to- point to a hub –
and-spoke model in logistics sector, eventually helping to bring down logistics costs and 
enabling more efficient movement through new -generation vehicles. The importance of a 
modern and effic ient logistics network cannot be overemphasized. Poor connectivity across 
various logistics modes not only increases the wear and tear of transport means and damages 
to goods, but also leads to uncertainty in supply chains leading to further decrease in th e 
route utilization by trade and thus, increasing transportation costs for the remaining users. 
Sagarmala aims at construction of wider roads for connectivity of Ports to another point. 
However, unfortunately, the Committee noticed that in some cases the S agarmala Projects 
are undertaken only up to major crossroads on the route and thereafter no effort is made to 
construct road up to point envisaged in the Sagarmala Project. The Committee is constrained 
to note that in such a situation the wider roads/conne ctivity between the Port and the point 
envisaged in the Sagarmala Project beyond the point of cross roads will remain unfulfilled. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the point –to–point Sagarmala connectivity 
envisaged may be implemented irrespective  of the fact that there exists major cross roads in 
between. The Committee stresses that road connectivity under Sagarmala should not be only 
point to point but encompass the entire peripheral network of roadways interlinking nearby 
towns, villages, servic e roads, important tourist places, national monuments etc. for the 
overall development of the areas. The Committee emphasizes that service roads should be 
included in the DPR itself, and given as much importance. 
(Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The suggestions of the Committee are noted. Further, it is submitted that better port 
connectivity facilitates efficient cargo movement between ports and their respective 
hinterlands minimizing overall logistics cost of the country. The Ministry of Ports, Shippin g, 
& Waterways endeavours to enhance road and rail connectivity to all ports having sizeable 
traffic. The enhancement of port connectivity is an ongoing and continuous process. Under 
PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan, more infrastructure gaps are identif ied to link the ports 
end-to-end with the existing/ upcoming major economic zones/ industrial clusters/ nodes/ 
corridors with an objective to holistically integrate all the multimodal connectivity projects

and remove missing gaps for seamless movement of people, goods, & services.
