4. The Chairman welcomed the senior officers of the GMR Group, DIAL, and APAO to the 
meeting and informed them that the Committee had heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry 
of Civil Aviation (MoCA), Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI), and Director General, 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) on the subject ‘Development of Greenfield, and 
Brownfield Airports and Issues pertaining to Civil Enclaves in Defence Air ports’ in its earlier 
meetings held on 16th and 25th November, 2022 and now by engaging with the stakeholders, 
whose agreement is a vital element in construction of airports,   hoped to get valuable 
suggestions and inputs on the challenges faced by them.   The Chairman asked the 
representatives of DIAL and APAO to share their suggestions on the existing rules/regulations 
and policies pertaining to the development of Greenfield/Brownfield airports in the country, the 
                                                           
2  Relates to other matters 

130 
 
bottlenecks faced by them, key challenges f aced in conducting various airport operations, 
administering the availability of finances and obtaining clearances especially regarding Public 
Private Partnership (PPP) mode of operations of the airports, problems of capacity saturation of 
airports and the need for long-term planning, lacunae existing in various processes of the Indian 
Civil Aviation Sector, viz., documentation, financing, taxation, technical aspects, sub -
agreements or contracts, internal and external interfaces, etc., and suggest possible solutions and 
improvements required in Concessionaire Agreements. 
 
5. Thereafter, the Chairman queried about the coordination mechanisms employed 
by  DIAL and APAO with various government agencies, such as, AAI, DGCA, Airports 
Economic Regulatory Authority (A ERA), Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) etc. and 
other private aviation stakeholders to resolve issues related to security and maintenance of 
aviation standards, crowd control, airports security checks, aeronautical tariffs, development fee, 
and carrying out various operations in Greenfield/Brownfield airports across the country. The 
Chairman also asked the representatives of APAO to put forth their views on the levying of 
‘Facilitation Fee’ by authorized travel agents on air ticket booking on govern ment accounts. The 
Members of the Committee also desired to hear the views of other Private Airport Operators 
especially Kochi, Bengaluru and Kannur Airports and also expressed that in future, the Heads of 
the organisations should appear before the Committee for interactions.  
 
6. The GMR Group representing the DIAL, through its presentation, informed the 
Committee of   its experience in airport operations, with two existing airports in India being 
operated by them, viz.   Brownfield airport in Delhi   and Greenfield airport in Hyderabad and a 
third airport, the newly inaugurated Greenfield airport in MoPA, Goa to be operationalized next 
month as well as a proposed   Brownfield airport in Nagpur and a Greenfield airport in 
Bhogapuram (Visakhapatnam). Outside India, the Group  operates a Greenfield airport in Cebu, 
Philippines and a Brownfield airport at Medan, Indonesia apart from developing a Greenfield 
airport in Greece, which will be ready in the next three years. 
 
7. Elaborating on the difficulties faced by private operators, the representatives of the GMR 
Group informed the Committee that timely resolution of tariff issues was a major problem and 
took as much as six years even though the appellate mechanism in the AERA Act stipulates that 
disputes are to be settle d within 90 days.    The reason is that such issues are settled by the 
Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) which also has jurisdiction over 

131 
 
telecom disputes and cyber issues and   is unable to allot sufficient time to airports.   A separate 
appellate tribunal meant for airports or a dedicated bench with the TDSAT may solve this 
problem.  The second issue was lack of provision of long -term financing by the Indian banks to 
airport infrastructure projects which have long gestation periods.   Comparing the gestation 
period of 50 years for the DMRC at   low interest rates, it was suggested that participation of 
Pension Funds, Development Finance Institutions, Insurance companies such as Life Insurance 
Corporation of India (LIC), etc. be allowed/ facilitated to provide long -term financing at 
competitive rates of 8-10 percent to the Indian airport sector.   
 
8. On the issue of improvement of terminal infrastructure, it was suggested that allowing a 
common security area for both arrival and departure would achieve optimum utilization of assets 
with lower capital cost while reducing airport challenges for passenger s. The representative also 
highlighted the requirement of planning of infrastructural projects outside the airports, citing the 
problem of water logging at Delhi International Airport due to drainage issues on the roads 
outside the airport. Comparing the c argo handling of India and Hong Kong, the representative 
asserted that transshipment should be allowed to enable India to become a Cargo Hub. He also 
raised the issue of allowing Input Tax Credit on civil construction, arguing that it would enable 
airport charges to decrease as 70 percent of airport construction is civil cost.    It was also 
suggested that Credit facility on the Emergency Credit system should be extended for   the entire 
aviation sector including all the allied adjacent businesses.  
8. Regarding the comparative advantages and disadvantages of Greenfield and Brownfield 
airports, the Committee was informed that Greenfield airports, having the advantage of hassle -
free development due to lack of o bstructions and security hassle s but the risk of litig ation and 
time taken in R&R system is higher as compared to Brownfield airports.   Regarding suggestions 
on amendments to existing legislations, the representative opined that the regulatory mechanism 
of the AERA Act, should be made more attractive and a se parate Act for PPP projects should be 
made as more development in future is to be through PPP routes.   Easing the process for land 
acquisition and environmental clearances in construction of airports, enhancing Duty -Free 
allowance  as a passenger-friendly measure, bringing out a legislation to curb/address the stray -
dog menace around the airport peripheries, etc were also suggested.   
 
9. The Committee was also informed about the security concern caused by the 
encroachment of defence land located near the Delh i International Airport. The Committee was 

132 
 
further informed that freedom should be given for movement of civilian aircraft   in order to 
avoid detouring and wastage of Air Turbine Fuel (ATF).   
 
10. Regarding the query of the Chairman on implementati on of Conce ssionaire Agreement, 
it was opined there should be an enabling provision for need -based consequences and the 
agreement should be amended wherever the requirement arises. Regarding another query of the 
Chairman on the coordination mechanisms employed by the Group with various Government 
Departments, the Committee was informed that the Group had to deal with 55 agencies of both 
the Central and State Governments but is getting a lot of support from them.  
 
11. The Chairman observed that the problem of capacity saturation at airports is a major 
issue and asked the GMR Group the reason the problem had not been envisioned 
beforehand.  The Committee was   informed  that the existing capacity of Delhi airport is 70 
million and a master plan was devised in 2019 to increase it to 109 million by 2023.   The 
Committee was informed that steps have been taken to minimize congestion at airports viz. 
increasing X -ray screening points from 13 to 17, employing additional staff for queue 
management, enhancing communication inside airports, employing ‘on e-passenger-one-
handbag’ policy, installing artificial intelligence (AI) -based waiting time display systems and 
communicating with various airlines to reduce peaks -hour operations, etc and a significant 
reduction in waiting time was already being seen.  
 
12. The representatives of APAO also informed that the shortage of manpower in CISF, the 
Immigration and the Air Traffic Controllers has also been hampering the airport operations for 
the last couple of years and causing airport congestion. All three being rese rved activities of the 
Government, the staff has to be provided by the Government but there were no service level 
agreements for CISF and Immigration staff.   Upon query by the Chairman, the Committee was 
further informed that presently, Rs 200/ - is being charged per domestic passenger as Aviation 
Security Fee (ASF) which goes into the National Aviation Security Fee Trust. This amount is 
later distributed equally to all the airports by AAI. This mechanism was devised to distribute 
funds equally as smaller a irports in India having less passenger traffic were not getting enough 
funds. However, in bigger Airports where more CISF staff is required due to more passenger 
traffic, there is always a shortage of such funds and this also results in congestion due to l ack of 
security personnel.  A Member pointed out that the Government has abolished 3000 CISF posts 

133 
 
as technology had made them redundant. The Chairman asked that a more detailed note may be 
given on this issue for study by the Committee.  
 
13. The Committee ex pressed concern at the issue of congestion at Delhi International 
Airport and the inability of the airport operators to handle this situation. A Member pointed out 
that Airports are bound by the Operation, Management & Development Agreement (OMDA), 
Schedule III of which states that 95% of the passengers have to be cleared through checking -in 
within 10 minutes. However, most of the passengers spend much more than 10 minutes time. He 
also stated that as per the Schedule IX of the said Agreement, there is a pe nalty clause of 1.5% 
of the monthly revenue and enquired whether the DIAL has been penalized yet under the 
Schedule IX.   The Committee also desired that the possibility of installation of full body 
scanners at all major airports may be explored for faster clearance of passengers. 
 
14. The Chairman also pointed out that all the passengers are made to pass through the 
commercial shopping complexes at airports and many Members were of the opinion that, even 
allowing for the Revenue Model, provision of essential fa cilities to passengers should be the 
focus rather than shopping areas.   The representative submitted that due to the OMDA

into as a potential source of funding for airport projects.

Government can frame a policy without consulting the State Governments compelling them to 
contribute land free of cost without expecting any equity. The Finance Secretary opined that it is 
desirable to consult State Governments in such cases. He added that the Government is often 
able to take up individual cases in a slight deviation from the policy because the policy is n ot a 
law.

requests for the development of an airport even if there is desirability or possibility of the Central

Government to build the airport. The Finance Secretary  stated that the policy is binding on the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Finance but the Union Cabinet can go beyond the 
policy. 
13.       The Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs stated that all fairly viable airports can 
be taken up by the private sector but beyond big cities, there is an issue of viability. He informed 
the Committee that adding the cost of land to the project would result in a large number of 
projects becoming unviable. He cited the example of railway projects wherein hu ndred per cent 
cost of the land for any new line to be constructed, is to be borne by the State Government, along 
with 50 per cent of the project cost. He added that the Department of Economic Affairs had not 
commented on Para 13(a)(iii) of the NCAP at the time of consultation regarding the policy.

provide land even in case an airport project is viable. Another Member highlighted the issue of 
almost all airports in t he North -Eastern States being unviable and sought to know about the

Aviation should ask for viability gap funding in case of unviable projects, not force upon the 
State Governments to provide land free of cost.

any specific comment about Para 13 when it was referred. He stated that the promotion of 
competitive and collaborative federalism is one of the cornerstones of NITI Aayog which is why

Report 
Culture is the soul of any nation, and it is our duty to preserve, nurture, and promote our rich 
cultural heritage. In India, we are blessed with a diverse tapestry of cultures, languages, traditions, 
and art forms that have been passed down through generations. It is essential that we ensure the 
proper functioning of our cultural institutions, such as the various Akademis, which play a crucial 
role in preserving and promoting our cultural legacy. 
2. The primary mandate of the Ministry of Cult ure (MoC) is the preservation and conservation 
of ancient cultural heritage and the promotion of tangible and intangible heritage. MoC through its 
organizations is engaged in  the development of the country's rich heritage including art, music, 
dance, theat re, literature, and handicrafts as well as recognition of excellence in these fields. The 
Akademi Bureau of MoC has the overall administrativ e supervision of the following a utonomous 
bodies viz. Sangeet Natak  Akademi, Sahitya Akademi, National School of Dr ama, Lalit Kala 
Akademi, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts a nd 
Kalakshetra Foundation. 
3. The Cultural Akademis are the most prestigious in the country and yet there is a growing 
apprehension that they have failed to fulfil their original mandate and have been ineffectual in 
popularising the arts among the  general population. The Committee notes that the promotion of arts 
and culture through Akademis and other Cultural Institutions lacks an integrated approac h since 
there are a host of overlapping functions. This results in duplication of efforts and prevents the 
optimum utilisation of resources. Allegations of administrat ive mismanagement and financial 
irregularities have been levelled against some of the Aka demis. Further, the issue of 
bureaucratisation of the functioning of cultural Akademis which stifles their creative dynamism 
arises from time to time. 
4. The Committee decided to examine these premium Cultural Institutions to understand their 
functioning a nd how to make them more accountable, effective, visible and relevant, without 
impairing their autonomy in any manner. During the course of the examination, the Committee heard 
the Ministry of Culture, Administrative Heads, and elected Heads of National Akademis and other 
Cultural Institutions in its meetings held on 9th May, 2023 and 29th May, 2023, respectively.

I 
Objective and Mandate of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
5. Mandate of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA), was set up in  1952 as India's national ac ademy of music, dance 
and drama. It is  functioning as the apex body in the field of performing arts in the country, 
preserving and promoting the vast intangible heritage of India's diverse culture.  
Sahitya Akademi  (SA), India’s National Akademi of Letters , established in 1954 by the 
Government of India is the central institution for literature, literary dialogue, publication and 
promotion of literature in the country and the only institution that undertakes literary activities in 24 
languages including English. Sahitya Akademi confers 24 awards for original and creative writing 
every year.  
Lalit Kala Akademi  (LKA) which was inaugurated in 1954, is the N ational Academy of Art and 
Culture and focuses its activities in the field of visual arts  such as sculpture, graphics, ceramics and 
painting. It is an autonomous body, fully funded by the Ministry of Culture.  
The National School of Drama  (NSD) is one of t he foremost theatre training institutions in the 
world and the only one of its kind in India. It was set up by the Sangeet Natak  Akademi as one of its 
constituent units in 1959 and in 1975 became an independent, autonomous organisation fully 
financed by the Ministry of Culture.   
Centre for Cultural Resources and Training  (CCRT), established in 1979 is one of the premier 
institutions working in the field of linking education with culture. CCRT conducts a range of training 
programmes for in-service teachers, educators and administrators across India. 
The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA), established in the year 1987 is a major 
resource centre for arts and functions as a centre for research, academic pursuit and dissemination in 
the field of arts.  
Kalakshetra, as the name suggests, is a centre for artistic endeavour. Founded in 1936 by the vibrant 
visionary Rukmini Devi Arundale, the institution stands testimony to her dream of creating a space 
where the essence of Indian thought would find e xpression through artistic education, an institution 
she established with the vision “of imparting to the young the true spirit of Art, devoid of vulgarity 
and commercialism.”

6. Achievements, Programmes and Initiatives of the National Akademis 
The Ministry submitted the following  with regard t o the efforts and ende avours of the Akademis in 
pursuance of their respective mandate: 
Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA), has been working relentlessly to achieve its mandate to preserve and 
promote the performing art forms of the country. It has successfully achieved its goal by promoting the 
performing arts through audio -video documentation, publications, and by supporting and promoting as 
well as recognizing the artists by giving production and publication grants, by organizing festivals, 
seminars, etc., at various levels, and through Akademi Fellowships and Awards for artists of all age 
categories. 
The Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) is an institution that has rendered service to the nation in the sphere of 
arts long before the world woke up to the global impact of Indian art.  Central to the Akademi’s mission 
is the encouragement of a deeper understanding and enjoyment of modern and contemporary art by the  
diverse local, national and international audience that it serves.  It is involved in a wide range of 
activities related to the promotion of art and artists through programmes and strategic partnerships by 
organizing Camps/ Workshops / Lecture s/ Seminars/Art Festivals/Exhibition/ Residency 
Programme/Cultural Exchange Programme/ Competition /Film Shows/Slide Shows etc. 
The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) has the mandate of propagation of Culture 
in Schools and Colleges and has provided training to 2,13,659 teachers across the country. The institute 
also ensures its presence in every corner of the country, under its District Resource Person (DRP) 
Scheme by appointing its trained teachers as DRP s who ensure the dissemination of art and culture at 
the grassroots level. Till date , CCRT has trained 10,11,497 under the “Extension Services and 
Community Feedback Programme”. 
The National School of Drama (NSD) has already trained over 1200 theatre Postgraduate Diploma 
students in the performing arts, not only in India but throughout the globe. Beside s regular teaching and 
training programmes, the premier drama institute also engages in extension activities and reaches to the 
nooks and corners of the country by extending support to theatre practitioners and theatre workers. NSD 
has consistently produced thespians and popular artists of silver screen and most of the students get 
employed in the respective fields of direction, production, acting and lighting etc. 

Page 4 of 88 
 
Sahitya Akademi  (SA), in the endeavour, to fulfil its objective of promoting literature has been 
conducting workshops seminars and felicitating talented writers of all age group s by conferring awards. 
Sahitya Akademi also undertakes translation of literary works in 24 Indian L anguages thereby 
popularizing the literature of one region across the country.  The Akademi has also published 7000 
books in 24 languages in the last seven decades.  It publishes original works and also works in 
translation-fiction, poetry, drama, essays an d criticism -covering classical, medieval, pre -modern and 
contemporary literature. 
The Indira Gandhi National Centre (IGNCA) for the Arts serve s as a major resource centre for the 
arts, specially written, oral and visual source materials. It has achieved maj or milestones in 
digitalization activities relating to manuscripts, microfilming, photographs, and reference cards. IGNCA 
has major functions and specializes as a R esearch Centre and has been in charge of supervising the 
installation of new artworks in the new Parliament. 
Kalakshetra Foundation (KF) has been steadfastly maintaining the standard and tradition of training 
in Bharatanatyam, Carnatic Music and craft education and the institution has been successful in 
popularizing the classical art forms in Ind ia and abroad. Most of the students have become successful 
and popular artists in their respective fields.

Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
16. The Ministry informed the following with regard to the election and tenure of the Heads of 
the National Akademis: 
Sahitya Akademi (SA) 
The President of the Sahitya Akademi  is selected by the new General Council from a max imum 
three-person’s panel to be forwarded by the outgoing Executive Board. The outgoing Executive 
Board selects the panel from the names forwarded by the outgoing General Council. The President 
continues in office until the election of the new President by the new General Co uncil at its first 
meeting. The General Council has 100 representatives from different sources. The State 
Governments and Union Territories send three nominations each.   The Ministry also receives 
nominations of three names each from all 350 Central and St ate Universities where Humanities are 
being taught,  out of which representatives of twenty universities are selected on a rotation basis.   
There is also a provision for 24 language representatives and about 10 ex -officio members like Joint 
Secretary etc. The authority vests in the General Council of the Akademi which also elects the 
President of the Akademi for a period of five years. 
 
Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) 
The Lalit Kala Akademi  is an autonomous body, fully funded by the Ministry of Culture. It 
comprises of the General Council and Executive Board for three years and the term of the Chairman 
is for three years.  Chairman, Lalit Kala Akademi is appointed through a 3 -Member Search 
Committee, (one member is nominated by the General Council of the Akademi and the other two 
members shall be nominated by the Pre sident of India; and one out of three members may be a 
woman). The Search Commit tee submits recommendations of three  names to the President of India.  
The President of India appoints one out of the three names for Chairmanship. The General Council 
of the Akademi consist s of 65 Members.  The term of the members of the Executive Board as are 
elected by the General Co uncil or nominated by the Government of India or the Chairman for 
membership of the Executive Board is three years.

Segregation of Functions   
53. The Committee notes that t he Ministry of Culture through its organizations is engaged in the 
development and promotion of the country’s rich heritage including art, music, dance, theatre, literature 
and handicrafts as well as recognition of excellence in these fields.  The different autonomous cultural 
institutions have been tasked with specific components of  culture.  The Akademi Bureau of the Ministry 
of Culture has the overall administrative supervision of these autonomous bodies. 
54. The Committee feels that the function of the Akademis is to enable artists to create and 
express their creativity.  The role of the Ministry should be to help the organizations and their 
artists to realize the organizational vision and fulfil their mission. Its responsibility is to provide an 
atmosphere for artists to develop and realize their vision with resources that would otherwise be 
unavailable or greatly diminished in the face of lack of opportunities. The Committee notes that 
the 2014 High Powered Committee also expressed  that the Ministry has to work as a point of 
coordination for cultural expression and a catalyst for the dissemination of that expression 
through the encouragement and sponsorship of multifarious artistic activity . To t his end, 
Committee feels that there should be proper and clear segregation of functions among the 
Akademis. 
55. The Committee observes that segregation of functions is  also an important concept to 
internal control frameworks, financial reporting and regula tory compliance. The overall 
effectiveness of the organization depends on an effective internal administration, adequate division 
of responsibilities, and the requirement of a sufficient number of staff who are adequately trained.  
Separation of functions is an important mechanism to help reduce the risk of fraud, error and 
other financial misconduct .  In addition , it helps to promote accountability, transparency and 
ethical behaviour within the organization.  The Committee, therefore, recommends segregation of 
the purchasing, provisioning, financing and policy-making functions within the Akademis.

atmosphere for artists to develop and realize thei r vision with resources that would otherwise be

The Committee notes the instances of recipients of awards, given by Akademis (such as Sahitya 
Akademi Awards), returning their awards in protest of certain political issues which are outs ide 
the ambit of the cultural realms and the autonomous functioning of the concerned Akademi. Such 
inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the achievements of the other 
awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the awards. 
(Para 92) 
A Member of the Committee opined against the view that artists, authors and other intellectuals 
and performers who have been recommended for awards must sign a commitment that they will 
not return the awards as a form of protest at any point in the future before they are able to receive 
it. He was of the view that India is a democratic country, and our Constitution has provided to 
every citizen the freedom of speech and expression and also the freedom to protest in any form. 
Returning of awards is only a form of protest. The Member added that the Committee must 

Page 51 of 88 
 
strongly recommend to the Government to look into the actual issues in protest of which such 
awards have been returned and work towards resolving them. He was seconded by anoth er 
Member.  
(Para 93) 
The Committee questioned the re -engagement of such awardees who joined the Akademi after 
insulting it. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the awards. 
The Member again submitted that the Akademis and the other Institutions should continue to 
work together with these artists and not shun them.  
(Para 94)  
The Committee observes that the awards given by each Akademi continue to be top honours for 
an artist in India. The Committee emphasizes that Sahitya Akademi or other Akademis are 
apolitical organizations. There is no place for politics. The Committee, therefore, suggests that 
whenever an award  is given, the consent of the recipient must be taken, so that he/she does not 
return it because of political reasons; as it is disgraceful to the country. The Committee 
recommends prior concurrence of short-listed candidates for awards before finalization.  A system 
may be put in place where an undertaking is taken from the proposed awardee citing acceptance 
of the award and that the awardees cannot dishonour the award at any point of time in future.  
Awards may not be given without such an undertaking. In  the event that the awards are returned, 
the awardee shall not be considered for such award in the award in the future. 
(Para 95) 
Community participation and public awareness 
In Committee’s opinion, artistic and cultural activities can engage a wide audien ce in a way that 
resonates with their cultural background. They are an effective forum for community 
collaboration and engaging marginalized communities.   
(Para 102) 
The Committee feels that there is a need to strengthen ties with local communities, artis ts, and 
cultural organizations. Further, a bottom -to-top approach is required for a better understanding 
of the ground level requirements. Akademis should involve communities in decision -making 
processes, co-creation of programs, and the preservation of in tangible cultural heritage. Engaging 
with the community helps ensure relevance and authenticity in cultural activities, further, leading 
to the revival of lost traditions, languages and customs. 
(Para 103) 
Public-Private Partnership (PPP): 
The Committee fe els that little has been done in engaging the private sector and there is still a 
wider scope for exploration in this field. Private partners can provide financial support through 
sponsorships, grants, donations, or investments. Private partners can also p rovide expertise, 
resources, and technical assistance to the Akademis.  Collaboration with private partners in the 
co-creation and co -production of programs, exhibitions, festivals, or other cultural events can 
bring diverse perspectives, innovative ideas, and broader networks to the cultural Akademis. 
(Para 108) 
 

Page 52 of 88 
 
 
Protection of rural and tribal culture 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry. The Committee feels that the 
specialized body for Rural, Tribal and Folk Arts could if set up, be a vehicle for the propagation of 
folk and tribal art forms effectively. This would also mean nurturing these forms and preserving 
them in their original form as well as encouraging innovation in presentation without destroying 
the authenticity of th ese art forms. This could perhaps also be a way to raise the status as well as 
the remuneration of these artists to levels comparable to those of the classical artists. In addition, 
it can facilitate a cultural dialogue between all art forms from classical to traditional. 
(Para 117) 
The Committee also believes that it is important to prioritize the voices and perspectives of tribal 
communities, while also providing platforms for them to share their culture with a wider 
audience. Akademis should develop educational outreach programs that promote tribal and rural 
culture in schools, colleges, and local communities.  There is also a need for  collaboration with 
tribal organizations, NGOs, and tribal development agencies to jointly support initiatives for the  
promotion of tribal culture. Further, Akademis must promote rural stays and tribal stays, 
especially among the younger generation to acquaint them with the cultural heritage of the 
country. 
(Para 118) 
Youth engagement 
The Committee notes that the efforts are largely targeted at getting children to learn art forms – 
namely dance and music. The Committee feels that intervention is required to make them aware 
of what these traditions are; at least to a point where they can identify some very basic ideas of th e 
performing and visual arts. While the Ministry of Culture set up the CCRT with somewhat a 
similar idea of reaching out and creating opportunities for young children, especially from smaller 
cities, and all regions including the North -East, the program ne eds to be seriously reviewed and 
updated. Further, it should be linked with other ongoing efforts of the Ministry. 
(Para 121) 
Leveraging G20 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry of Culture and various cultural 
institutions in showcasing India’s rich cultural heritage and art forms at various G20 forums and 
Conferences. The Committee observes that this is a golden opportunity to propagate and exhibit 
our thousands of years old continuous cultural heritage to the world community. 
(Para 127) 
The Committee recommends that Akademis should collaborate with tourism authorities and G -20 
stakeholders to promote cultural tourism in India.  Akademis should also  encourage G -20 
delegates to explore Indian cultural treasures beyond the conferenc e venues, thus promoting 
tourism and economic opportunities. Akademis can initiate collaborative projects between 
National Akademis and cultural institutions from G -20 member countries. This can involve joint 
exhibitions, performances, artist residencies, or cultural exchanges. Digital platforms like social 
media handles, live streaming, and virtual exhibitions can be utilised to extend the reach of

National Akademis cultural initiatives during the G -20 summit and to engage a global audience 
and promote cultural exchange beyond physical boundaries. 
(Para 128) 
Members of the Committee also raised various other issues which are as follows: 
 i. Incentives for artists showing their talent on trains, buses, etc.: 
Some people beg for money in trains, buses in exch ange of a devotional song, a qawwali or a 
melodious Bollywood number. While most of them are physically challenged, some just take up 
the practice out of sheer poverty. However, many of these beggars are also musically trained or 
belong to families that ha ve been practising music for generations together. Ministry/Akademis 
must take measures to identify such artists and provide them a platform to showcase their talent 
and also provide monetary support to them. 
(Para 129(i)) 
ii. Representation and promotion of culture of North East States of India: 
North East India is known for its geographical location, ecology and diverse culture. It is the 
homeland of large number of ethnic groups. Each ethnic community has its own distinct culture 
including food, music, d ance, dress, language, etc. However, despite this, the North East has not 
been represented to the degree it deserves to be represented. Ministry must take measures in this 
direction and implement more schemes to preserve and promote various forms of art an d culture 
in the NER. Ministry must extend all kinds of assistance including financial support to the 
individual artists and organizations in this region. 
(Para 129(ii)) 
iii. Handling, preservation and digitization of Manuscripts: 
 Manuscripts are the prim ary source of historic information. Manuscripts are diminishing along 
with time. Despite their best efforts, it is difficult to save manuscripts in a physical form beyond a 
time frame. Digital preservation of manuscripts restores them from damage, larceny and decay. 
The Ministry should evolve a well -designed digitization program that includes not just digital 
capture, but also appropriate care and repair of original materials, and long -term management of 
the digital files it produces. 
(Para 129(iii)) 
iv. Need for promotion of art and culture in schools: 
Arts in modern education help to stimulate creativity, inspire confidence, and foster personal 
growth. It is a necessary part of any student’s education and should be encouraged in all schools. 
Indian arts of  all kinds must be offered to students at all levels of education, starting with early 
childhood care and education. Outstanding local artists and crafts persons should be hired as 
guest faculty to promote local music, art, languages, and handicraft, and t o ensure that students 
are aware of the culture and local knowledge of the region where they study. 
(Para 129(iv)) 
v. Lack of career guidance programmes in the arts for school children: 
Most teenagers are receiving little to no career guidance outside the home. Choosing a career path 
after school can be challenging, especially for students who have pursued arts. However, with the

growing demand for creative and artistic talents in various  industries, the career options for art 
students have increased significantly. Arts need no longer remain a passion and hobby. Career 
option guidance programmes must be encouraged in schools to help students who want to pursue 
a career in the arts and creative field full-time. 
(Para 129(v)) 
vi. Non-availability of information in Hindi or any other local language: 
Culture is encased in our languages. Art, in the form of literature, plays, music, film, etc. cannot 
be fully appreciated without language. In ord er to preserve and promote our diverse culture, we 
need to preserve and promote a culture’s languages. Further, information on the art and culture 
must also be made available in Hindi and the local languages. 
(Para 129(vi))

2.         At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and informed them that the 
agenda of the meeting was to deliberate on the subject of “Functioning of National 
Akademies and other Cultural Institutions”. The Chairman also informed the Members 
that as the Secre tary, Ministry of Culture had sought exemption, the Committee would 
instead hear the Joint Secretary of the Ministry along with the administrative heads of all 
the National Cultural Akademies. 
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.           The Chairman noted that the Akademies have been given autonomous status to 
ensure their freedom of expression but issues of bureaucratisation of the cultural 
institutions which hampers their creative dynamism arise from time to time.   The 
Chairman asked that the Committee may be briefed on this issue as well as the challenges 
faced due to lack of infrastructure, manpower shortages and bureaucratic hurdles. He 
asked the Ministry and Akademies to elaborate on the measures taken to promote and 
preserve cultural traditions in the digital age.  The Chairman also noted that there were 
allegations of administrative and financial irregularities in the functioning of some of the 
Akademies, especially the Lalit Kala Akademi and desired that the Committee may be 
briefed in this regard. The Chairman asked the JS whether the budgetary support provided 
by the Ministry to each institution/Akademi is adequate to meet their needs and whether 
any financial assistance is provided to artists/scholars by the Akademies/Ministry.   Citing 
an article in a newspaper  wherein Ministry officials were quoted as stating that Cultural 
Akademies should mobilize funds only from non -governmental sources and not depend 
on government funding, the Chairman enquired about the legality of such proposals.    
4. The Joint Secretary informed the Committee that there were seven Cultural 
Akademies, the oldest being Kalakshetra Foundation (founded in 1936), then the Sangeet 
Natak Akademi (established 1952), the Sahitya Akademi and the Lalit Kala Akademi 
(both established in 1954), the National School of Drama (NSD) (established 1959), the 
Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT) (established in 1979) and the newest 
being the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) (established in 1985).  

92 
 
5.         The mandate of the Kalakshetra Foundation is mostly   Bharatnatyam and Carnatic 
Music while the Sangeet Natak Akademi promotes the intangible heritage of dance, 
music, and drama.   The Sahitya Akademi   promotes literature, including   children's 
literature. The Lalit Kala Akademi   is  working on tribal traditional arts and ceramic art.   
The NSD is working in the field of theatre. The CCRT is working for educating   school 
children on culture. The IGNCA works as a repository of all the art forms in the country 
and does a lot of research and documentation..   
6.         In response to a query by a Member, the representative of the Ministry informed 
that the tenures of Chairmen/ Presidents are different for different Akademis. In the case 
of Lalit Kala Akademi, the tenure is three years. The NSD and the CCRT are having four 
years tenure. IGNCA has the longest tenure of ten years while the remaining three 
Akademis have a tenure of five years.   Each Akademi, since they are autonomous bodies, 
has its own General Council and an Executive Board. 
7.         In response to another query about the election of the Chairman/President of the 
Akademies, the representative of the Ministry explained that the process was again 
different for different Akademies.  The Chairman of Lalit Kala Akademi is a presidential 
nomination chosen from a list of 3 -4 experts in the field of art picked out by a  Search-
cum-Selection Committee, which is appointed by the Ministry.   The General Council has 
65 members drawn mostly from the n ominations received from each State/ Union 
Territory as well as the nomination of 5    members from the Government of India and ex -
officio members like the Joint Secretary (Akademis) and the Finance Member.   All the 
members have voting rights and decisions are taken on majority vote.  
8.         The President of the Sahitya Akademi, usually a person of eminence in the literary 
field, is elected by the General Council. The General Council has 100 representatives 
from different sources. The State Governments a nd Union Territories send three 
nominations each.  The Ministry also receives nominations of three names each from all 
the about 350 Central and State Universities where Humanities are being taught,   out of 
which representatives of twenty universities are selected on a rotation basis.  There is also 
a provision for 24 language representatives and about 10 ex -officio members like Joint 
Secretary etc.   Upon a query by a Member, it was informed that there were only 20 
members in the University category and car e was taken during selection to include all 
States on a rotation basis since some states had only one university.  

93 
 
9.       The Sangeet Natak Akademi has 72 members, with one representative nominated 
by each State Government in addition to experts, governm ent nominees and ex -officio 
members.  
10.       The National School of Drama and Kalakshetra are mainly training institutes. The 
Chairman of the NSD is appointed by the President while the NSD Director is a 
Government appointee.   Both are appointed by the Government from among three 
candidates selected by a search cum selection committee.    
11.  The Chairman remarked that there are different parameters for different Akademies 
and there is a need to bring uniformity among all the Akademies in terms of tenur e of 
Chairmen/President and representation and election of General Council members.    The 
representative of the Ministry acknowledged that as most Akademies have been   in 
existence  since the 1950s, there is a need to change the age -old systems and the Ministry 
has  taken cognizance of the same 
12.     The representative of the Ministry also informed that the IGNCA has   9 centres 
across the country, the Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi 
(SNA) have 7 each, and the Sahitya Akademi and the  NSD have 5 each while CCRT has   
4.  Upon query by Members about the reason for no centres being in states like 
Rajasthan, the Ministry informed that Zonal Cultural Centres cater to cultural needs in 
places which do not have Regional Centres. Besides, the Akademies and CCRT conduct 
shows and workshops even in places where are no centres.   
13. A Member enquired about the mechanism of preservation and promotion of the 
intangible culture of India. He gave examples of artists from around the country, the lack 
of recognition of their work and the ways to promote their work. The Ministry elaborated 
on their efforts to promote the unsung heroes of India like the event of Jyotirgamaya of 
Sangeet Natak Akademi in Rajasthan which comprised 350 artists for five days. 
Similarly, an event in Delhi focussed on instrument making. Upon further discussion and 
observations by some Members about the lack of visibility of the programmes and 
workshops conducted by the Ministry, the representative of the Ministry stated that the 
entire information about the last three years of the programmes, workshops and other 
activities done in Rajasthan and other states would be provided   institution-wise.  A 
Member suggested that  a meeting can be held once in three months in the State Capital  

94 
 
about the working of the Akademies to which    Members of Parliament   can also be 
invited.    
14. Upon a Member’s query whether the Akademies have tribal members the JS informed 
the Committee that the Ministry promotes all States’ art forms and any tribal art expert 
nominated by the State Government, is taken as a member.  
15.       The Committee was further informed about the achievements of the various 
Cultural Akademies - 
 the Sahitya Akademi held   India’s largest international literature festival – 
UNMESHA in Shimla under the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (AKAM) , that hosted 
64 events featuring more than 400 writers and scholars and the Festival of Letters 
in New Delhi which featured more than 400 writers, hosted 40 events and 
promoted 60 languages.      The Akademi also maintains the   archives for Indian 
literature and every year conducts more than 50 regional, national and 
international seminars and 100 symposiums and about 400 literary gatherings in 
every language. 
 the Kalakshetra Foundation inaugurated a 'Bharata Kalakshetra Auditorium,"    
free-of-cost dance classes for children in low socio -economic strata, Seminars and 
workshops to propagate craft, culture and education,  Kalanubhava, a First-ever art 
exhibition by  Rukmani Devi College of Fine Arts and a cultural festival at 
Mahabalipuram in presence of Hon’ble President of India and His Highness King 
of Netherlands etc.  
 Achievements of the NSD included the International Theatre Festival of India 
(Bharat Rang Mahot sav) where 100 theatre groups from India and abroad 
participate every year in February since 1999, National Theatre Festival organised 
for children (Jashn -e-bachpan & Bal Sangam), organises Indian Classical Drama 
Festival since 2016, Poorvottar Natya Samaroh since 2009 
 the achievements of the IGNCA   included the National Mission of Cultural 
Mapping, New Parliament artwork and the Vedic Heritage Portal,   Mera Gaon 
Meri Darohar (MGMD) initiative to document 6 lakh+ villages on various cultural 
parameters, lik e documentation of Devnarayan Phad tradition, the revival of the 

95 
 
art form of Ramman in a Joshimath village and in instrument making, the revival 
of original Tanpuras in Dharwar and many instruments of the North-East.  
 the achievements of the LKA included o rganising art camps and exhibitions and 
workshops and award of fellowships to artists selected from all over the country. 
 the achievements of the   Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards includes, organising the 
15th Sattriya Sangeet Samaroh to increase awareness ab out the Sattriya Music 
tradition, four-day music/dance/drama festival-Amrit Yuva Kalotsav for recipients 
of the Yuva Puruskar, organizing Jyotirgamaya where artists can register 
themselves on the SNA website with proof of their talent.   
  Under the CCRT’s initiatives  2,13,659 teachers have been trained since inception 
till date and 10,11,497 students were trained under ‘Extension Services & 
Community Feedback Programme.’ 14,637 and 1,908 scholarships were awarded 
under Cultural Talent Sea rch Scholarship Scheme (CTSS) and Scholarships to 
Young Artistes (SYA) Schemes respectively. 2,142 Junior/Senior fellowships 
were awarded from 2014 to till date. CCRT has also produced 57 publications and 
46 documentary films.  
16. The Committee was also i nformed that all the Akademies were contributing 
substantially for the Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (AKAM).   A programme called Kalanjali 
is being held regularly at the Central Vista where there are performances of various art 
forms and music bands. 
17.       The Committee was informed that a budgetary allocation of Rs. 31.413 Crores has 
been made to various Akademies, in which Rs. 59.75 Cr. is given to SNA, Rs. 95.84 Cr. 
to IGNCA, Rs. 53.91 Cr. to NSD, Rs.37.22 Cr. to Sahitya Akademi, Rs.26.84 Cr. to 
LKA, and R s. 22.67 Cr. to CCRT. The Chairman sought information about the detailed 
budgetary allocation to all Akademies for 2023 -24 and the reasons for low allocation and 
whether the Ministry consulted all the Akademies before the allocation of budget.  
18.       Upon enquiry by the Chairman about the allegations of financial irregularities in 
Lalit Kala Akademi prompting the Government's takeover of the Akademi in 2015, the 
representative of the Ministry informed the Committee that whenever a full -fledged 
Chairman is not selected, the Ministry appoints its representative for an interim period 
and there is no taking over of the institution.   A new Chairman has been recently 
appointed in the Lalit Kala Akademi.   Regarding the financial irregularities, the Ministry 

96 
 
undertook to inform the Committee after gathering the specific facts. The Chairman also 
enquired about the issue of the return of Awards by the artists, the number of such

synergy among Akademies, community participation and public awareness in the 
promotion of Indian culture. 
19.       Members raised various queries such as: 
 Filling up of vacancies and increasing funding for cultural akademies/institutions 
in the country; 
 Criteria for admission into NSD 
 Incentives for artists showing their talent on trains, buses, etc.;
